      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#introduction",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#introduction",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThis framework provides a set of principles and activities to guide the responsible development, procurement and use of data and artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector. It helps public servants understand ethical considerations and how to address these in their work.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eData and AI ethics is about using data and data-driven technologies responsibly, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erespecting privacy\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epromoting fairness\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprotecting individuals, communities and society from harm\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis includes ensuring that data is collected, shared and used in appropriate, fair, safe, sustainable and transparent ways.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe framework applies to any project that involves:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata (collection, sharing or use)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata-driven technologies\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAI\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eautomated decision-making and algorithmic tools\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this guidance, this is what we mean when we refer to ‘data and AI’.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"who-this-guidance-is-for\"\u003eWho this guidance is for\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe framework is for people who work in government and other public sector organisations. It’s mainly written for people who are designing, building, maintaining, using or updating projects that use data and AI.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis may include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edevelopers\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eproject managers\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eanalysts\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003estatisticians\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epolicy makers\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecommercial or procurement professionals\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe also encourage anyone who works directly or indirectly with data and AI to read this guidance and apply it to their work. This includes operational staff and anyone helping to produce data-informed insight.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"how-to-use-this-guidance\"\u003eHow to use this guidance\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should work through the framework together as you plan, implement and evaluate a project. You should regularly revisit it throughout your project, especially when you make changes to your work or project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe framework covers a broad range of use cases and challenges that you might encounter. Some projects may be limited to certain aspects – for example, data collection and processing – while others may cover a full AI development life cycle. This means you might find certain parts of this guidance more or less relevant to your project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"data-and-ai-ethics-self-assessment-tool\"\u003eData and AI Ethics Self-Assessment Tool\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf your team is working on an AI or data-driven technology project, then as well as reading this guidance you should use the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework\"\u003eData and AI Ethics Self-Assessment Tool\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe tool will help you capture information, and share learnings, challenges and progress with colleagues. We recommend that you maintain it along with your other project documentation to record decision making across the life cycle of a project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"why-this-guidance-is-important\"\u003eWhy this guidance is important\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment guidance needs to address the rapidly evolving ethical challenges and risks posed by data and AI technologies. We’ve updated the previous version of this guidance to meet this need.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Data and AI Ethics Framework bridges the gap between high-level ethical principles and practical actions. It considers themes such as safety, security and privacy through an ethical lens. It does not replace technical or regulatory guidance in these areas, but instead complements and connects to them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt complements existing tools, standards and guidance, including the:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html\"\u003eAI Playbook for the UK Government\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/data-ethics-guidance/the-model-for-responsible-innovation\"\u003eModel for Responsible Innovation\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub\"\u003eAlgorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (\u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis guidance does not replace:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eexisting ethics guidance and tools for statisticians and social researchers, such as the UKSA’s \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/the-authority-board/committees/national-statisticians-advisory-committees-and-panels/national-statisticians-data-ethics-advisory-committee/ethics-self-assessment-tool/\"\u003eEthics Self-Assessment Tool\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebespoke guidance provided by individual departments, devolved administrations or for specific professions\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"principles\"\u003ePrinciples\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is an overview of the main principles everyone should follow when working with data and AI in the public sector. The rest of the guidance explores each principle in more detail.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"transparency\"\u003eTransparency\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eTransparency means that information about your project, actions, processes and data are communicated to relevant parties in an understandable, easily accessible and free way. Transparency includes the concept of explainability, which refers to the ability to understand and communicate how a system makes decisions, including how it arrived at an individual decision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"accountability\"\u003eAccountability\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAccountability means that data and AI projects have appropriate and effective governance, oversight, and routes to challenge decisions in place, where this is necessary. It involves setting clear roles and responsibilities, and being transparent about the system and the processes around it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"fairness\"\u003eFairness\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness means avoiding unfair biases and impacts, and addressing accessibility barriers, while actively maximising positive impacts. You should assess data representativeness, bias, and the different potential impacts that can result from data use.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should mitigate model biases and aim for outputs and decisions generated with the help of automated processes to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebe non-discriminatory\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebe just\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erespect dignity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ealign with the public interest, human rights and democratic values\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecomply with the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance\"\u003eEquality Act 2010\u003c/a\u003e and the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities\"\u003ePublic Sector Equality Duty (\u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"privacy\"\u003ePrivacy\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrivacy means that personal data is respected and handled responsibly, ensuring it’s used only for intended purposes with an appropriate legal basis. It also means adhering to UK data protection regulation, including principles of data minimisation, purpose limitation and informed consent.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"safety\"\u003eSafety\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSafety refers to the use of data or development of a system without causing harm to people, organisations, wider social institutions or the environment. Data-driven systems such as AI should be robust, secure and safe at every stage of their life cycle. This means ensuring that they operate properly and reliably, without causing unnecessary safety or security risks.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"societal-impact\"\u003eSocietal impact\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSocietal impact is about how the development and use of data and data-driven technologies impact wider society. For example, by helping to solve societal challenges and deliver public good.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"environmental-sustainability\"\u003eEnvironmental sustainability\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSustainability calls for responsible design and use of data and AI that minimises environmental impact, and supports long-term wellbeing for people and the planet. This means considering biospheric consequences when scoping potential AI and data projects, and building tools and systems that are robust and energy efficient. Biospheric consequences are the effects a project can have not only on the planet’s ecosystems but also its climate and the entire biosphere.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"trade-offs\"\u003eTrade-offs\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere may be instances where you find that 2 or more of the ethical principles are in tension with one another. For example, using more demographic information may help to identify biases and promote fairness, but this may come at the expense of an individual’s privacy. Here, you might need to consider trade-offs. Ethical trade-offs are inherently complex and you must treat them with care.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere are some approaches which can help you establish suitable trade-offs:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einclude stakeholder perspectives by engaging with affected communities to understand values and impacts\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsult legal and human rights frameworks to ensure that decisions align with national and international standards\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebalance proportionality and necessity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensure meaningful and inclusive deliberation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eestablish mechanisms to monitor outcomes, and adjust if necessary\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"
      }

    {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "Transparency",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#transparency-section",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#transparency-section",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eTransparency is foundational to all other ethical principles. Being transparent allows for scrutiny of actions, decisions and processes. It cultivates accountability and can help to build trust in the use of data and technology. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eExplainability applies specifically to AI systems and the ability to describe how a system arrives at a given output or decision. For example, this could include explaining what factors led to a benefit application being granted or denied. Explainability can help to build trust by making it easier to understand decision-making processes, and easier to identify risks, inaccuracies and harms. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA lack of transparency might lead to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esolutions being designed suboptimally – at worst leading to harmful outcomes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einsufficient accountability and no clear ways to appeal decisions of automated systems – which may result in public distrust\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe first data protection principle in the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-and-the-eu/data-protection-and-the-eu-in-detail/the-uk-gdpr/\"\u003eUK General Data Protection Regulation (UK \u003cabbr title=\"General Data Protection Regulation\"\u003eGDPR\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e is that of ‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’. In the context of data protection, transparent processing is about being clear, open and honest with people from the start about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewho you are\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow and why you use someone’s personal information\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-transparency-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat transparency means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt can be helpful to think about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhy you’re being transparent\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat you’re being transparent about\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eto whom you’re being transparent\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor why you’re being transparent, consider these questions:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eare you following a particular mandate or requirement to be transparent? \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eare you trying to address topics such as safety, trust, accountability, internal or external scrutiny, reproducibility, transferability or robustness​?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat are the potential consequences of not being transparent?​\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow will your organisation balance the resources required to make material transparent with other competing operational priorities?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor what you’re being transparent about, consider:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe tools you’re using – for example, for data analysis or automated processes – and explaining the process or context for how you’re using them\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epublishing open data or source code, where this is safe and complies with internal governance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eexplaining the factors that influence a system’s output\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eproviding contact details to get in touch with your team\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn terms of who you’re aiming to be transparent to, consider:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einternal transparency within your organisation – for example, record-keeping for handover and continuity purposes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecross-organisational transparency – for example, sharing case studies with other government departments\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etransparency as part of oversight requirements – for example, being transparent to regulators, auditors or evaluators\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etransparency with directly affected individuals or defined groups – for example, explaining algorithm-assisted decision making\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epublic transparency – for example, publishing information about a project on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"http://gov.uk\"\u003eGOV.UK\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eDepending on who you’re trying to be transparent to, you should engage with these people and organisations. Ask them what type and level of transparency would be most meaningful and useful to them. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis might involve:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etalking to users about what level of explainability is useful\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etalking to civil society about what they need to know to effectively hold you to account\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etalking to researchers about what information would help them evaluate the system\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etalking to other teams in government about what information they would like about what you’re doing\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese considerations will help you identify the right content and level of transparency to use in each specific case, across relevant stakeholder groups. As an example, you might be the owner of a data set that others might benefit from, and which does not contain personal data. You might consider publishing it openly on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"http://data.gov.uk\"\u003edata.gov.uk\u003c/a\u003e. However, where personal data is concerned, you may have to provide transparency information in response to a data subject access request via official channels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs another example, if you want to ensure a smooth handover of an in-house AI system, you might choose to record and share its technical details and source code with colleagues. This will ensure it remains safe, functional and easy to maintain. Or, if you’re generating explanations of a system’s outcome to affected parties, you may adapt transparency information to include simple, non-technical and user-accessible explanations where possible.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"transparency-in-the-context-of-data\"\u003eTransparency in the context of data\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eData transparency is about communicating:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhere the data comes from\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow the data is collected, cleaned, used, stored, shared, analysed and interpreted\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe limitations of the data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow you’ve complied with applicable laws – for example, data protection and intellectual property law\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis applies to the data itself, but also to metadata (such as file format or author) and paradata (data about the data collection process itself). \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBeing transparent about data can involve the following elements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"open-data\"\u003eOpen data\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eMaking data openly available can support trust and transparency by allowing others to replicate and scrutinise published results. If data is non-sensitive, non-personal, and if data sharing agreements with the supplier allow it, you should make the data open and assign it a \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.doi.org/\"\u003edigital object identifier (\u003cabbr title=\"digital object identifier\"\u003eDOI\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou can publish government data sets on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"http://data.gov.uk\"\u003edata.gov.uk\u003c/a\u003e, following the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-data-charter\"\u003eOpen Data Charter\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"documentation-about-the-provenance-collection-or-generation-of-data\"\u003eDocumentation about the provenance (collection or generation) of data\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you’re collecting or generating data, it’s important to be open about why, what and how (by which methods) data is being collected.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"documentation-about-any-pre-processing-to-address-limitations-of-the-data\"\u003eDocumentation about any pre-processing to address limitations of the data\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eDiscuss what pre-processing steps you’ve taken to ensure adequate data quality. Disclose any limitations of the data, such as quality issues, missing or incomplete data, gaps in representativeness, or known errors.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"documentation-about-how-the-data-is-used-in-a-specific-project\"\u003eDocumentation about how the data is used in a specific project \u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen using data in a specific project, clearly communicate the problem domain, user need, project aims and value to relevant stakeholders. When starting data analysis, you should be able to clearly explain the purpose and methodology of your analysis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"documentation-about-data-sharing-and-access\"\u003eDocumentation about data sharing and access\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eBe open about who has access to the data, what data sharing agreements are in place, and what the conditions for reuse are, such as licensing.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"data-protection-related-transparency\"\u003eData protection-related transparency\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere personal data is being processed, you must comply with relevant laws: You need to carry out a \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/\"\u003eData Protection Impact Assessment (\u003cabbr title=\"Data Protection Impact Assessment\"\u003eDPIA\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e before you process personal data when the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. It’s good practice to publish your completed \u003cabbr title=\"Data Protection Impact Assessment\"\u003eDPIA\u003c/abbr\u003e to demonstrate that you’re taking the appropriate precautions to protect personal data and ensure your system is fair.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen processing personal data, you must provide a privacy notice that is easy to locate and explains in clear, accessible language:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhy you need the data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow long you’ll keep the data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhether you’ll share the data with others\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow people can exercise their rights or raise complaints\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should also explain the safeguards that achieve effective \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/\"\u003edata minimisation\u003c/a\u003e, such as anonymisation or pseudonymisation, in plain language.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eConcepts such as data sheets or data set cards can be helpful in recording some of this information. Good examples include \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.09010\"\u003edata sheets for data sets\u003c/a\u003e and variations of data set cards that have been developed based on this approach, such as \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://github.com/PAIR-code/datacardsplaybook/blob/main/templates/DataCardsExtendedTemplate.pdf\"\u003eGoogle’s data cards\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor more information, refer to the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/\"\u003eUK \u003cabbr title=\"General Data Protection Regulation\"\u003eGDPR\u003c/abbr\u003e guidance and resources\u003c/a\u003e on the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) website.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"fairness-related-transparency\"\u003eFairness-related transparency\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must comply with the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities\"\u003ePublic Sector Equality Duty\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance\"\u003eEquality Act 2010\u003c/a\u003e. This means you need to carefully consider and document the equality impact of processing \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/personal-information-what-is-it/what-is-personal-data/what-is-personal-data/\"\u003epersonal data\u003c/a\u003e where it can be used to identify individuals as having a protected characteristic. This document is often referred to as an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA). For more information, consult the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed\"\u003eEHRC guidance on the Public Sector Equality Duty\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt’s good practice to publish your EIA. This will demonstrate that you’ve considered the potential equality implications (both positive and negative) of processing data that relates to any protected characteristics. Publishing your completed \u003cabbr title=\"Data Protection Impact Assessment\"\u003eDPIA\u003c/abbr\u003e and EIA will build trust in your use of data and data-driven technologies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"transparency-in-the-context-of-ai-and-algorithmic-tools\"\u003eTransparency in the context of AI and algorithmic tools\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eEnsuring transparency and explainability can be complex in the context of AI, algorithmic and automated systems. Transparency can be limited by ‘black box’ algorithms or proprietary commercial tools. Explainability may not be possible for certain forms of machine learning, or may only be achievable at the cost of performance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo be transparent in the context of AI and automated systems, you should consider the following concepts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"technical-transparency\"\u003eTechnical transparency \u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is information about the technical operation of the AI system, such as the code used to create the algorithms and the underlying data sets used to train the model.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"process-transparency\"\u003eProcess transparency \u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is information about the design, development and deployment decisions and practices behind your AI solutions, and the mechanisms used to demonstrate that the solution is responsible and trustworthy. This may also include an audit log of the prompts and outputs generated by AI systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo enable process-based transparency, you should have the following in place:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erobust reporting mechanisms\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprocess-centred governance frameworks\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAI assurance techniques\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"outcome-based-transparency-and-explainability\"\u003eOutcome-based transparency and explainability \u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis means the ability to clarify to any person who is using or impacted by a service that uses AI, how the solution works, and which factors influence its decision making and outputs. This includes individual-level explanations of decisions, where this is requested. It can also include aggregate statistics about outcomes that can be used to monitor fairness.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"explainability-in-practice\"\u003eExplainability in practice\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor certain types of machine learning models, such as deep learning or large language models (LLMs), it can be impossible to fully explain the logic behind an output or decision due to their complex, ‘black box’ nature. For example, LLMs may \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government\"\u003ehallucinate\u003c/a\u003e (where LLMs generate plausible but factually incorrect information) for unexpected reasons. The size and complexity of these models may make it difficult or impossible to identify a determinate causal chain for why this has happened.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should assess the degree of explainability that’s necessary for your project given its specific domain context and use case. Do this before making technical or architectural decisions about the type of algorithmic techniques you’ll employ in model development. For instance, in high-impact contexts such as social care or criminal justice, you might need a higher level of explainability to ensure fairness and comply with applicable regulation. Considering explainability needs will help you avoid investing in inappropriate technology.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn other cases, where it’s impossible to understand or interpret the rationale behind the outputs of the model, consider alternative methods of explainability such as visualisation techniques or counterfactual explanations. The ICO has guidance on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/explaining-decisions-made-with-artificial-intelligence/\"\u003eexplaining decisions made with AI\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"using-the-algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard\"\u003eUsing the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub\"\u003eAlgorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (\u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e establishes a standardised way for public sector organisations to publish information about how and why they’re using algorithmic tools.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll central government departments and arm’s length bodies that provide public or frontline services, or routinely interact with the general public, \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-mandatory-scope-and-exemptions-policy/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-atrs-mandatory-scope-and-exemptions-policy\"\u003emust use the \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/a\u003e. This involves documenting information about any algorithmic tools used in decision-making processes, and making this clearly accessible to the public.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe also recommend the \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e to other public sector bodies, such as local government, even if they’re not currently mandated to use it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEven where a tool does not strictly fall within scope of the \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e, we recommend \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub\"\u003epublishing an \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e record\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"if-youre-using-a-third-party-supplier\"\u003eIf you’re using a third-party supplier\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eVendors of AI systems must be able to clearly explain:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe steps they take to build tools\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe logic and assumptions built into their tools\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow their tools generate outputs\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis explanation should include information about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe data used to train the AI model \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe function of the AI models\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe system’s intended purpose\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe steps they’ve taken to mitigate risks\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eBefore entering into a contract, consider asking your supplier:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow they engaged with users and affected communities across the development life cycle\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow they identified, evaluated and mitigated risks\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat the source of the data is\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow the data sets were created\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat data the model has been trained on\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif training data sets are sufficiently representative to facilitate fair performance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhere third-party data has been used to train the AI, if the organisation has a valid and lawful basis for processing\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif there are any known biases in the data or the trained model\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow accurate the system is\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif the system has been tested for differential performance on relevant demographic groups\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif the system is based on an LLM, what the observed rate of hallucinations is, and under what conditions they normally occur\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat benchmarks or other modes of model assessment and evaluation have been used to measure safety, reliability, robustness, performance, privacy preservation, toxicity and bias\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif there are any issues likely to affect quality\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should update the answers to these questions when significant changes are made to data sets, models, APIs or other relevant components that you’re procuring.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor further guidance on procuring AI systems, refer to the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government\"\u003eAI Playbook\u003c/a\u003e and the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning\"\u003eResponsibly buying AI guide for councils in England\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should consider any tools you’re procuring from a third party which are intended to be used in decision-making processes. These tools might fall within the scope of the mandatory requirement to use the \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e. At the stage, it’s helpful to ensure that the supplier is providing you with all the required transparency information requested in the \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou can also check the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://senseaboutscience.org/responsible-handover-of-ai/\"\u003eResponsible Handover Framework\u003c/a\u003e to identify the information needed for a successful AI system handover from supplier to buyer.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"recommended-actions\"\u003eRecommended actions\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should: \u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eexplain the what, how and why of your project in plain language to a non-expert audience; if you cannot articulate how the use of data or AI solves a defined problem, you should consider alternative solutions\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintain detailed records of the project – include the decisions that were made in its design, for example:\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow the project delivers positive social outcomes for the public\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat the user need is that it tries to address\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewho the senior responsible owner of the project is\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow a relationship with a third-party supplier was set up \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eyour EIA and \u003cabbr title=\"Data Protection Impact Assessment\"\u003eDPIA\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emake information publicly available – consider where you can make information about a project or tool publicly accessible, such as on GitHub, in blogs, on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"http://gov.uk\"\u003eGOV.UK\u003c/a\u003e or on your organisation’s webpage\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse the \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e if your organisation is within mandatory scope, and consider publishing an \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e record even if your organisation is not in mandatory scope\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003egive appropriate disclosure when AI has been used to produce an output – this concerns both internal and external uses of AI\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emaintain detailed records of all data sources used, including collection methods, licenses and pre-processing steps\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003epublish DPIAs and EIAs where possible – refer to the \u003ca href=\"#fairness-section\"\u003eFairness\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"#privacy-section\"\u003ePrivacy\u003c/a\u003e sections for more information\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emaintain detailed records of all the design decisions and assumptions that went into the development of a solution\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ecreate and regularly update assurance documentation that explains the model’s purpose, performance limitations and intended use cases – this might include model cards or data set cards\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eif possible, publish your source code openly – for example, on GitHub\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ebuild algorithmic tools with explainability in mind – consider how important explainability is for the intended use case, and the degree of explainability that would meet domain-specific expectations and regulation\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euse technical methods for assessing the interpretability of machine learning models – you should have a good working understanding of their limitations:\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecommon explainability techniques such as \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/\"\u003eSHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://c3.ai/glossary/data-science/lime-local-interpretable-model-agnostic-explanations/\"\u003eLIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations)\u003c/a\u003e may be helpful in some cases, but may be ineffective for, and inapplicable to, LLMs and generative AI systems\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsult technical experts and state-of-the-art research when choosing appropriate explainability methods\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"
      }

      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "Accountability",

        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#accountability-section",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eAccountability involves setting clear roles and responsibilities and being transparent about decisions. It means that people and organisations are responsible for the data they collect, use and share, and for the technology they build. It also means that if something goes wrong and a system or process harms someone, this can be raised and fixed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBeing accountable helps keep people safe, and ensures that data and AI is used fairly and responsibly. A lack of accountability or failure to uphold ethical standards can result in serious consequences, including:\n- unaddressed harm to people, such as unfair decisions\n- harm to public services\n- legal risks and repercussions\n- regulatory action\n- reputational damage and a loss of trust in organisations\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-accountability-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat accountability means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should take the following steps to establish and support accountability across a data or AI project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"set-clear-roles-and-responsibilities\"\u003eSet clear roles and responsibilities\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou need strong oversight and clear responsibilities to ensure accountability across the life cycle of your data or AI project. You must set out who is responsible at each stage of the project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis includes naming:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner\"\u003esenior responsible owners (SROs)\u003c/a\u003e – as the primary risk owners for the project, they ensure a real policy or business need is being addressed, engage with stakeholders and assure ongoing viability\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata owners – data sets must have named data owners accountable for quality, access controls and life cycle governance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata stewards – they should be responsible for metadata and day-to-day quality controls\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata custodians – they should be responsible for capturing, storing and disposing of data in line with the data owner’s requirements\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAI asset owners – they should be responsible for AI outputs, including model predictions and any generated data\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor project governance to be effective, it’s essential that the people accountable have appropriate technical expertise and knowledge, and authority, to implement necessary changes. This is especially important for complex projects or those involving multiple suppliers, which is often the case with data and AI projects.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor more information, refer to the:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/service-manual\"\u003eService Manual\u003c/a\u003e – which explains how to build a digital and data team\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ddat-capability-framework.service.gov.uk/#it-operations-job-family\"\u003eGovernment Digital and Data Profession Capability Framework\u003c/a\u003e – which outlines the skills needed for any digital and data role\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eguidance on \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner\"\u003ethe role of the SRO\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/project-delivery-functional-standard\"\u003eGovernment Project Delivery Functional Standard\u003c/a\u003e – which sets expectations for the management of government projects\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eguidance on \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-shared-data-assets-and-data-ownership-in-government/data-ownership-in-government-html\"\u003eData Ownership in Government\u003c/a\u003e – which sets out a data ownership model that formalises the roles of the people in government responsible for managing data throughout its life cycle\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"traceability-and-auditability\"\u003eTraceability and auditability\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour project team should keep clear records to show how your data or AI system was designed, developed and used, who made a decision and the evidence they used. This will make your project accessible for audit, oversight and review by appropriate parties. It will help others check that your work is trustworthy, and that it meets legal and ethical standards.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor any project that uses data, your team must:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ename an SRO and data owner for the data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eestablish who is responsible for each component of the project, including third-party vendors\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edocument lawful use and purpose of processing, including legal basis and a recording of processing activities\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eregister new data assets – either via organisational data catalogues, or cross-departmentally by designating \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-shared-data-assets-and-data-ownership-in-government/essential-shared-data-assets-esdas-guidance-for-departments-html\"\u003eEssential Shared Data Assets (ESDAs)\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erecord and retain audit trails of who has access to the data and why\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erecord all important decisions and maintain a process log with evidence of responsible data practices\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprovide routes for people to raise concerns, complaints or request corrections\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo ensure AI and algorithmic systems can be audited or reviewed, your team must:\n- record who is responsible for each part of the system, including suppliers\n- keep information about where the data came from and how it was used – from data collection and preparation, to training, testing and use\n- record decisions made during project design, model deployment and system deployment processes\n- keep clear records that show how the system was designed, developed, tested and implemented\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis information should be easy to find and understandable to a range of stakeholders. For example, a data set factsheet can help explain how data was handled. The \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-template\"\u003eAlgorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (\u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e also provides a template for public sector organisations to document and share information about how and why they’re using algorithmic tools.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you’re building an AI system, you should take steps to ensure that the system is explainable. For example, you can explain why a model or algorithmic tool has produced a particular outcome. There are some cases where it can be difficult to trace the inputs and outputs of AI systems, such as large language models (LLMs). The \u003ca href=\"#transparency-section\"\u003eTransparency\u003c/a\u003e section has more information on explainability.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"establish-feedback-mechanisms\"\u003eEstablish feedback mechanisms\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eUpholding accountability means ensuring that people affected by the use of a data or AI system can:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eunderstand how decisions were made – this may include data sources, decision-making criteria and logic\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprovide feedback\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econtest outcomes that are incorrect\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eseek redress if they‘ve been affected by erroneous or unjust outcomes – for example, by asking for the decision to be reviewed or corrected, especially in the case of automated decision making\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should create a clear mechanism for monitoring the ongoing use of your data or AI project. This involves evaluating how it’s used, and providing a feedback loop where users and operators can identify issues and send them back to the development team.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should also set up a clear way of handling and responding to feedback, complaints and appeals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eExamples of feedback mechanisms might include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esurveys and feedback forms\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereporting mechanisms integrated into the tool or service\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003estakeholder workshops\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere appropriate, you should engage with civil society organisations for guidance on how to design and integrate feedback and redress mechanisms for your AI project or system.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"maintain-human-oversight\"\u003eMaintain human oversight\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003ePeople must be able to monitor and influence how systems work, even when the system is partially or fully automated. People should remain responsible for the decisions they make when these are supported or informed by an AI system.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf your system includes automated processing, make sure there’s appropriate human oversight. This includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erecording how much of the process is automated and how much is controlled by people\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003enaming the roles and people responsible for oversight and for managing risks\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eavoiding fully automated decisions where the outcome could significantly affect individuals or groups, and making sure a person makes the final decision in these cases\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif using LLM tools, ensuring someone is verifying outputs for incorrect information and potential biases\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn some AI use cases, automated decision making can be difficult to avoid. For example, it would typically be impossible for humans to review every conversational output of an LLM-based chatbot. Here you should weigh the risks of incorrect or harmful outputs and resulting negative impacts against the benefits of using the system.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn some cases, where the risks of potential harm and incorrect outputs are high, the right choice might be to not use the system at all. In other cases, you may want to put risk mitigations in place – for example, providing easy access to human agents if a chatbot malfunctions or is unable to help users.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eIf your project uses personal data\u003c/strong\u003e, you must meet your legal duties under the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-and-the-eu/data-protection-and-the-eu-in-detail/the-uk-gdpr/\"\u003eUK General Data Protection Regulation (UK \u003cabbr title=\"General Data Protection Regulation\"\u003eGDPR\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e. This includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebeing responsible for how personal data is used\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eshowing how you meet the data protection principles\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecompleting and documenting \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/\"\u003eData Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003efulfilling transparency obligations – including the publication of privacy notices or fair processing notices\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eenabling people to exercise their data protection rights\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour organisation’s data protection officer (DPO) or information assurance team should be able to advise on your data protection obligations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"accountability-if-youre-using-a-third-party-supplier\"\u003eAccountability if you’re using a third party supplier\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you buy a data-driven or AI system from a supplier, you must:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emake sure the supplier understands their responsibilities\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eagree what risks they must manage\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eask them to share information about how the system works\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs a baseline, make sure that any supplier maintains the same standards as would be expected from you if the system was developed internally. This applies to data governance, performance evaluation, data minimisation and legal accountability.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should include the following responsibilities in the contract:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eproduct liability – suppliers may be liable if the system causes harm because it gives unsafe outcomes or fails\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata liability – if the system breaks data protection or other applicable law or misuses data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ealgorithmic harm – if the system breaks equality law for discriminatory, biased or unfair outcomes, particularly in public services (such as social welfare or policing)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esecurity liability – liability for damage caused by insufficient security measures or third-party manipulation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003efailure to meet contract terms – including penalties, clawback clauses and potential contract termination\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einsurance – you can ask suppliers to have insurance that covers harm caused by AI\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor more guidance on procuring AI technologies, refer to the:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.crowncommercial.gov.uk/downloadable-resource/request/67557/buyers-guidance-supporting-the-procurement-of-artificial-intelligence-via-ccs-agreements\"\u003eBuyer’s guidance on AI procurement\u003c/a\u003e \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidelines-for-ai-procurement\"\u003eGuidelines for AI procurement\u003c/a\u003e \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning\"\u003eResponsibly buying AI guidance\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eUltimately, it’s important to keep in mind that the public body remains responsible for all data and algorithm-assisted decisions or outputs, and their impacts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"recommended-actions-1\"\u003eRecommended actions\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003enominate an SRO, typically a senior decision maker, to be accountable for the project\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003etalk to your organisation’s DPO and ensure they have the necessary information, tools and authority to govern the project\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eestablish mechanisms for independent reviews of your project to review and challenge decisions relating to data and AI systems, where appropriate\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eclarify legal responsibilities across the data and AI supply chain, ensuring that all parties involved in the data and AI project life cycle – from vendors and technical teams to system users – are acting lawfully and understand their respective legal obligations\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eif you’re buying a system commercially, define detailed responsibilities and liability contractually\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epublish information that’s accessible to technical and non-technical stakeholders, and explains:\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ehow your AI system works (including its purpose, data sources and decision logic) \u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ehow the actions and decisions you’ve taken across the entire AI project life cycle have ensured that it’s ethical, lawful and trustworthy\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ehave mechanisms in place for users to provide feedback, such as reporting errors or contesting decisions that might be inaccurate or harmful\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eestablish a human-in-the-loop process to oversee and validate outputs and decisions where AI is used in risky or high-impact situations – this person or team should be able to identify risks and intervene, where appropriate\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eidentify who is responsible for the outputs and decisions made by the AI systems you use, and assume responsibility if this is not clear – this includes interactions with LLM-based tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
