      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "Fairness",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#fairness-section",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#fairness-section",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eFairness is a diverse concept. It concerns both the way people are treated and described, and how opportunities and resources are distributed in society. Fairness is deeply rooted in our cultural, moral and political practices, and you should regard it as a good in its own right. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnfairness undermines social and economic opportunity and creates power imbalances. Inequality can undermine the legitimacy of government and erode trust. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnfairness in your project may result in:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eunlawful discrimination and other conduct prohibited in the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance\"\u003eEquality Act 2010\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003egrowing inequalities and community tensions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eregulatory, reputational and legal risk\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness in data and AI involves a combination of social, technological and legal concerns to determine whether people and organisations are treated justly, without systemic advantage or disadvantage.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government’s collection and use of data and implementation of AI systems have wide-reaching impacts on society. Each time a data point is collected or an algorithm deployed, it can have the potential to widen or close gaps in opportunity, representation and resources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"equality-and-inclusion\"\u003eEquality and inclusion\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eEquality and inclusion are fundamental ethical principles for fairness. Equality is about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensuring that all people have equality of opportunity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eexercising government functions in a way that’s designed to reduce inequitable outcomes stemming from socio-economic disadvantage\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must take care when ensuring equality in your project. Avoid any form of positive discrimination, as this is prohibited. Instead, take positive action such as targeted training and learning more about \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/positive-action-in-the-workplace-guidance-for-employers/positive-action-in-the-workplace\"\u003epositive action in the workplace\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInclusion is about ensuring that all groups can use and benefit from your project, accommodating for the needs of different physical and mental abilities and different contextual and cultural needs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-fairness-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat fairness means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness considerations are critical across the life cycle of your project – from initial decisions about what data to collect and how, to the impacts of your project years after deployment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo understand what fairness means in your project, first determine what aspects of fairness are most relevant to your project. For example:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif your project involves classifying events or objects – such as flagging fraudulent claims – the most relevant interpretation of fairness may be equal error rates between groups\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eif your system provides access to a public service or type of benefit – such as access to government grants for research – proportional access may be more important\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must understand and comply with your legal obligations and duties. Refer to the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed\"\u003ePublic Sector Equality Duty (\u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e and the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance\"\u003eEquality Act 2010\u003c/a\u003e. The \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e is made of a general duty across Britain, with specific duties that vary between England, Wales and Scotland. There’s guidance for public sector bodies on the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/new-guidance-ai-and-equality-available-public-sector-bodies?return-url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.equalityhumanrights.com%2Fsearch%3Fkeys%3DAi%2Bguidance\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e and AI\u003c/a\u003e and a \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/how-consider-equality-policy-making-10-step-guide-public-bodies-england\"\u003e10-step guide\u003c/a\u003e on how to deliver an Equality Impact Assessment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"call-to-action\"\u003e\n  \u003ch4 id=\"proxies\"\u003eProxies\u003c/h4\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eProxies are data points that are strongly correlated to other characteristics. For example, postcodes might be strongly correlated with age and race. While use of proxies is, in many instances, lawful, it’s essential to review data sets and models for proxies that may be introducing bias.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThis especially applies to bias against \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/equality/equality-act-2010/protected-characteristics\"\u003eprotected characteristics\u003c/a\u003e such as:\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cul\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eage\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003edisability\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003egender reassignment\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003emarriage and civil partnership\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003epregnancy and maternity\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003erace\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003ereligion or belief\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003esex\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003esexual orientation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003c/ul\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eSome attributes can be used to accurately infer a protected characteristic. For example, someone’s age can be inferred by their date of birth. Other attributes may be used to deduce a protected characteristic with varying degrees of accuracy – for example, postcodes that indicate likely ethnicities.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eProxies are not inherently harmful. For example, an organisation might use a proxy to monitor where a policy is having positive impact, or use that data to improve outcomes for people with protected characteristics where direct data does not exist.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eHowever, harmful outcomes can occur when a public body:\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cul\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eis not aware that the data it’s processing can be proxies for protected characteristics\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003edoes not consider the potential impact on people with protected characteristics\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003edoes not measure or remedy impacts, as this can lead to unlawful discrimination and reduced equality of opportunity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"understand-impacted-groups\"\u003eUnderstand impacted groups\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should understand which individuals or groups could potentially benefit or be treated unfairly by your project, and which are most vulnerable to harm as a result.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese may be groups that share a \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/equality/equality-act-2010/protected-characteristics\"\u003eprotected characteristic\u003c/a\u003e, or groups connected through different attributes such as their location, interests, the industry that they work in, and more.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnderstanding and assessing the impact that a project may have on people, particularly in relation to the protected characteristics, helps public bodies demonstrate they comply with the \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must assess the equality impact of your project:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebefore making any decisions to initiate a project, including procuring and development\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eduring implementation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eafter implementation\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere’s no set way for you to record your equality considerations and your organisation may have its own Equality Impact Assessment (EIA) template for you to complete. We recommend that your EIA follows the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/how-consider-equality-policy-making-10-step-guide-public-bodies-england\"\u003e10-step guide\u003c/a\u003e published by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC). This will help you navigate what you must do to comply with the law, and what you should do to demonstrate best practice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"call-to-action\"\u003e\n  \u003ch4 id=\"representational-and-allocational-harms\"\u003eRepresentational and allocational harms\u003c/h4\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eAnother way to understand fairness in your project is by considering the harms that it may cause. Harms are often categorised as either representational or allocational. Both concepts existed long before AI or data-enabled services, but technology means they may manifest in different ways and may need to be addressed differently.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eRepresentational harms concern how people are portrayed, including stereotyping, misrecognition and denigration. There are many cultural and institutional examples, such as in advertising, branding and entertainment. The impact of these harms can include reinforcing negative societal biases and social norms, psychological impacts and more.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eRepresentational harms are linked with the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed\"\u003ethird aim of the \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/a\u003e – ‘to foster good relations between people who have protected characteristics and those who do not’. Avoiding these harms will help you uphold your duty. \u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eDigital technologies, especially AI, are introducing new avenues for representational harms to occur. These harms are especially prevalent in generative AI models. The many different ways that AI may manifest in different types of content (text, video, image, audio) can make it particularly difficult to identify and mitigate.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eFor example, large language models (LLMs) are known to encode biases and stereotypes from the text that they’re trained on. This may result in displaying gender bias when describing certain job roles, or reproduce negative stereotypes associated with protected demographic groups. Meanwhile, AI models that generate images have been found to typically generate images of light-skinned men when prompted to produce images of CEOs and judges, perpetuating harmful biases.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eRepresentational harms can also emerge in data sets. For instance, over-representation of minority groups in crime statistics could result in unfair and unlawful treatment.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eAllocational harms are linked with the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed\"\u003efirst and second aims of the \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/a\u003e, and concern how resources or opportunities are distributed among society. In particular, they impact operational departments responsible for providing access to any kind of service or resource. Examples include citizen-facing services that give access to medical procedures or medicines, or structural systems like the allocation of funding to build new schools. The impact of allocational harms can include loss of opportunity, reinforcing and perpetuating inequalities, and more.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eYou should pay particular care to any algorithm employed where there are known historical inequalities, as the available training data is likely to encode these same biases. \u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThough representational and allocational harms are described as distinct areas, they often overlap in the real world. For instance, a hiring system that is biased towards hiring women into nursing roles displays both representational and allocational harms. It stereotypes nursing as a job conducted by women, and increases the likelihood that the employment opportunity is allocated to a woman.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"understand-downstream-impacts\"\u003eUnderstand downstream impacts\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e and any other fairness and equality requirements that you’ve identified for your work are ongoing. It’s important for you to regularly review the impacts that your work is having on people and society.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis can help you to determine whether:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eyou’re delivering the intended benefits you set out to deliver through your project, and that your investment is delivering value for taxpayers’ money\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eyour project is not leading to unintended consequences, including unlawful discrimination\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe actions you’ve taken to mitigate negative impact and maximise positive impact are having the intended effect\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eDownstream impacts can be hard to predict. User research and journey mapping can help you understand the downstream impacts of your project. Civil society organisations may be able to provide important insights on potentially impacted groups. They may also be able to support the recruitment of user research participants in difficult-to-reach communities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"building-for-fairness\"\u003eBuilding for fairness\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you determine that the risks and impacts identified in your EIA are acceptable, you’re likely to begin assembling a team to develop your project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHaving a diverse and multidisciplinary team can provide a strong foundation for building fairer tools and services. A diverse team is often able to spot issues early in the development process by bringing varied perspectives and lived experiences.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf it’s not possible to assemble a diverse team, you should note any potential gaps in understanding and proactively seek ways to engage with a variety of stakeholders. This might include through user testing, public engagement and, where possible, presenting ideas at internal or external community events.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should note the potential blind spots and pay attention to these in testing and in conversation with civil society groups.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should also apply these considerations when contracting out work to third-party organisations. For example, consider the diversity of their development teams and the methods they employ to mitigate potential gaps.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness metrics are different ways to measure whether your data set is representative and free from bias, and whether AI systems treat people equitably. They can help to identify and quantify biases, and inform further development to ensure outcomes are not disproportionately favourable or harmful to certain demographic groups. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should identify fairness metrics that are relevant to your project and address the potential harms you’ve identified. These can include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edemographic parity – where the proportion of positive or negative outcomes is the same for all groups\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eequalised odds – a measurement of the accuracy of results (true-positive rate and false-positive rate) across different groups\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness metrics are an evolving area. Each metric has relative strengths and weaknesses and research may uncover better methods. We recommend that you read current research on this topic to identify the most appropriate measurement for your project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you identify bias in your data or AI system, you must identify and implement mitigation techniques to reduce the risk and potential severity of harms. Apply these techniques anywhere in your project where bias occurs, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata collection and processing methods\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebias in any systems, including AI systems\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebiased impacts felt downstream\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eData on demographics, particularly related to protected characteristics, can support equality monitoring and meeting your obligations under the \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e. You should consider privacy here, referring to the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-and-data-protection\"\u003eguidance on the use of personal data to support the \u003cabbr title=\"Public Sector Equality Duty\"\u003ePSED\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"accessibility-and-fairness\"\u003eAccessibility and fairness\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness is not just about the outputs of your data set or AI system, but also about how people interact with the project and who can access and use it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt’s important to remember that a proportion of the population does not have access to the internet or devices such as smartphones and tablets. Some groups are more at risk of being digitally excluded, including older people and people with disabilities. Some users may prefer non-digital channels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis means that certain, often vulnerable, groups may not have access to digital services or be represented in data collected through digital platforms. As a result, their needs may be entirely missed or underrepresented.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should actively conduct research with groups that may be excluded to understand their needs. You should also provide non-digital alternatives where possible, such as phone support or paper forms.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll public sector websites and applications must adhere to the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/\"\u003eWeb Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 requirements\u003c/a\u003e unless they qualify for a specific \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2018/952/pdfs/uksiem_20180952_en.pdf\"\u003eexemption\u003c/a\u003e. Even for exempt services, the WCAG 2.2 still provides useful guidance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWCAG 2.2 provides information covering colour contrast, screen reader support, captions, and more. You should ensure that all content is written in plain language. Where appropriate, you should also make the content available in alternative languages and formats such as braille or British Sign Language. These and other similar changes may be considered \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/business/employing-people-workplace-adjustments/examples-reasonable-adjustments-practice\"\u003ereasonable adjustments\u003c/a\u003e. There are examples of reasonable adjustments applied to service delivery in the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/how-consider-equality-policy-making-10-step-guide-public-bodies-england\"\u003eEHRC’s 10-step guide\u003c/a\u003e. \u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"data-sets-and-labels\"\u003eData sets and labels\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFairness may be negatively impacted by bias in data sets, or bias emerging from the way a data set is transformed and used. Here are some of the ways in which your data sets may be biased.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"representation-bias\"\u003eRepresentation bias\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eData may be biased if it’s not representative – for example, not including enough examples from a particular group, or not including the group at all. This could cause higher levels of inaccuracy for impacted groups, leading to inaccurate decision making. It could also cause lower levels of performance, which may result in frustrating user experiences or barriers to accessing a service.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eMinority groups are inherently more likely to be underrepresented, which may lead to compounding negative effects. In these instances, oversampling (capturing more information about the concerned group) may be beneficial.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eCertain locations have historically been better researched than others. On a global scale, the Global North (North America and Europe) tends to be more represented in data sets when compared to the Global South (Africa, South Asia and Latin America). Within countries, major cities tend to be more highly represented when compared to rural areas and informal settlements.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"societal-bias\"\u003eSocietal bias\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eBias may still be present in a data set even if it’s fully representative of the population, due to biases present in our current and past society. Societal bias occurs when the data we collect, generate and use reflects discriminatory patterns present in society.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"data-aggregation-bias\"\u003eData aggregation bias\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eThis occurs when data is grouped or aggregated in a way that distorts the results of the analysis. For example, over-aggregating ethnic groups in demographic data – such as by only using ‘White’, ‘Black’, ‘Asian’ or ‘Other’ – can mask differences between groups, such as ‘Gypsy, Roma and Traveller (GRT) communities’.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe act of grouping data can obscure important variations and nuances present within the subgroups or individual data points, leading to a misrepresentation of the underlying relationships. Note that \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/fairness/?modulepage=design-biases\"\u003eaggregation bias in AI\u003c/a\u003e has a different meaning, referring to instances where trained models are applied in a one-size-fits-all manner. \u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"measurement-bias\"\u003eMeasurement bias\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003eThis arises from discrepancies between gathered data and real-world experiences or events. This can happen due to flawed measurement processes and inconsistent or inaccurate data labelling. Measurement bias may also \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/fairness/?modulepage=design-biases\"\u003ebe present in AI systems\u003c/a\u003e.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eData labelling practices (the process of assigning a tag, name or description to data to provide additional context) can also be a source of bias. Labels may be assigned inaccurately, and improperly designed labelling schemes may make it impossible to be accurate in all cases.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ongoing-fairness-commitments\"\u003eOngoing fairness commitments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour fairness commitments do not end once the project has gone live. Unforeseen problems may emerge in the real world. Shifts in the societal, cultural, economic and technological landscapes may mean that your project does not remain fair throughout its life cycle.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt’s vital that you continue to monitor the performance of your project post-implementation, including fairness and inclusion. You should include fairness and equality clauses in contractual arrangements with any third-party suppliers. Your monitoring should include information from suppliers if aspects of your project are procured or contracted out to third-party organisations. The Local Government Association has guidance on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning\"\u003eresponsibly buying AI\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should maintain user feedback and issue reporting systems throughout the system’s life, and make these visible to users. Consider what resources you should make available throughout the life cycle of the system, to fix newly identified fairness problems and to remediate harms. You should disaggregate your investigations into this feedback to understand the impact on different groups.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"disaggregated-feedback\"\u003eDisaggregated feedback\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAggregated feedback – the combined feedback from all the groups on your project – may help explain technical aspects of the project’s performance. However, it’s unlikely to tell the full story. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor instance, your project may involve a chatbot which receives 95% positive feedback from users. While this statistic may seem positive on the surface, it’s critical to understand which groups of people are satisfied, and which fall into the 5% that are dissatisfied. This may reveal that the dissatisfied group aligns with a particular protected characteristic. Identifying this provides an opportunity to mitigate impacts and build a fairer and more inclusive service.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub\"\u003eAlgorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (\u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/a\u003e provides a way to publish information about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003efairness metrics – for example, those included in your EIA\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eactivities such as testing and bias mitigations\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf your project involves an algorithmic tool that’s in scope of the standard, your transparency record could provide a strong platform to communicate the fairness attributes of your project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"recommended-actions-2\"\u003eRecommended actions\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edefine fairness – understanding what fairness and associated risks and opportunities mean in your project, and how you might measure that across its life cycle\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eunderstand your users – identify the groups most likely to be positively or negatively impacted by your project, and how this relates to the protected characteristics described in the Equality Act 2010\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003econsider which proxies might relate to the protected characteristics in your data set and be mindful and transparent about their use and purpose\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ecomplete an EIA and consider publishing it alongside your \u003cabbr title=\"Data Protection Impact Assessment\"\u003eDPIA\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e record (if relevant) for transparency and accountability\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003einclude diverse views – consider the diversity of your project team and any third parties you’re contracting\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ecollect feedback and data throughout your project to ensure that it continues to be fair and delivers its intended benefits, as society and user groups change\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eregularly update your EIA\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"
      }

      "@type": "Question",

        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#privacy-section",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003ePrivacy is a complex ethical, legal, technological and social principle. It protects individual autonomy, meaning people should have the freedom to live, think, choose, socialise and more without undue observation or interference. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn a digital and data-driven society, personal data is routinely collected, processed and used by public sector bodies to generate insights, develop AI tools and make decisions. This impacts peoples’ privacy and needs to be protected in line with ethical and legal obligations. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA failure to respect individuals’ privacy can lead to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eloss of public trust\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eharm to people, particularly vulnerable individuals\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eregulatory risk\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrivacy is not just a legal compliance exercise, but a fundamental human right that fosters trust and empowers individuals in the digital age. This guidance explores ethical responsibilities that extend beyond legal compliance, but you must still comply with the law at all times by following:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-and-the-eu/data-protection-and-the-eu-in-detail/the-uk-gdpr/\"\u003eUK General Data Protection Regulation (UK \u003cabbr title=\"General Data Protection Regulation\"\u003eGDPR\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/a\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2018/12/contents/enacted\"\u003eData Protection Act 2018\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/data-use-and-access-act-2025\"\u003eData (Use and Access) Act 2025\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eany other applicable privacy legislation\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-privacy-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat privacy means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must design and build privacy into your project from the start. This includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe very first decisions you make about what information you intend to record\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eevery way that the data, or AI system built using this data, is used throughout your project\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe safe decommissioning of the system and data set\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis concept is referred to in the UK \u003cabbr title=\"General Data Protection Regulation\"\u003eGDPR\u003c/abbr\u003e as \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/guide-to-accountability-and-governance/data-protection-by-design-and-default/\"\u003eprivacy by design and default\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrivacy is about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eautonomy – citizens’ capacity to live their own lives and make decisions based on their own motives and reasons, free from external manipulation (provided actions are within the law)\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003econfidentiality – data can be both sensitive and private, and confidentiality is the duty to ensure it’s only shared in appropriate and authorised ways\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003edignity – this is about the intrinsic value of all people, not as data points, but as people; it means ensuring that any methods of data collection, processing and use of AI do not exploit, humiliate or dehumanise people\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"purpose-and-benefit-in-the-context-of-data-protection\"\u003ePurpose and benefit in the context of data protection\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eBefore you start collecting, sharing or using data, you should clearly understand:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhy you’re processing the data (the purpose)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat public benefit this will bring\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe scope of your project should be strictly limited to your identified purpose throughout its life cycle. You should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eengage with your organisation’s data protection officer (DPO)\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003econsider whether your purpose could be easily understood by someone with no technical background in the domain – people must be able to understand your project so they can provide clear, informed and unambiguous consent\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eclearly record the purpose and benefit of your project – for example, who benefits, and how you’ll know if you achieve your aims\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eexamples of measures could include cost savings, reduced waiting times or the number of people who receive support\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eexplain why AI is the right tool for this purpose, if your project uses AI\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eArticulating and recording your purpose and public benefit at this stage can help to avoid scope creep and may help you comply with regulation such as the UK \u003cabbr title=\"General Data Protection Regulation\"\u003eGDPR\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"scoping-and-data-acquisition\"\u003eScoping and data acquisition\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf your project involves the collection or use of any personal data, you should start by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eestablishing precisely what information you need to meet your purpose\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecreating a high-level map of your data flow before this begins – for example, a document that lists each data element as a line item, and records why it’s necessary, proportionate and what the effect would be if it was not used\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe data you request and acquire must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which it is processed. This is known as data minimisation. The Information Commissioner’s Office has guidance on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/\"\u003edata minimisation\u003c/a\u003e, including how to determine if the use of data is adequate, relevant and limited.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eConsider whether you could use anonymised or \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-insights/ai-insights-synthetic-data-html\"\u003esynthetic data\u003c/a\u003e to replace some or all of the personal data your project requires. If personally identifiable information is essential for your project, ensure that the risks are proportional to the benefits.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour project might not itself gather or process personal data. For example, if you procure an AI model from a third party or use a pre-trained model. Here you must still ensure that any personal data used to train these models meets your privacy standards and complies with relevant legislation. The UK Statistics Authority (UKSA) provides an \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/ethical-considerations-relating-to-the-creation-and-use-of-synthetic-data/pages/6/\"\u003eEthics Checklist\u003c/a\u003e relating to the creation and use of synthetic data which may support these decisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Local Government Association has guidance on \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning\"\u003eresponsibly buying AI\u003c/a\u003e which discusses data protection.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"privacy-by-design-and-default\"\u003ePrivacy by design and default\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are 2 main principles to guide the development of your system or service:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eprivacy by design – making design and development decisions from the very start that enhance privacy objectives\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eprivacy by default - ensuring that default settings for the product or service are the most privacy-preserving options\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/privacy-enhancing-technologies-cost-benefit-awareness-tool/cost-benefit-awareness-tool\"\u003ePrivacy enhancing technologies (PETs)\u003c/a\u003e can help to achieve a privacy-by-design approach.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTransparency can also support privacy. Design methods and notices to explain:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat data you collect\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhy you need the data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow the data is used\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow long the data will be stored for\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eA good principle to uphold is that nobody should be surprised about how their data is being used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAI systems require greater attention and introduce new risks. For example, AI systems may re-identify individuals that were believed to be anonymised by linking information with other data sets, or information made available when it was trained. In addition, large language model (LLM) tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot may ‘memorise’ sensitive or personal information contained within their training data sets and leak this private information during their operation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo mitigate this risk we recommend that you: \u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etreat all models that have been trained on data about people as though they potentially contain personally identifiable data, and make security and risk-based decisions accordingly\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhere appropriate, manage access via an \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/application-programming-interfaces-apis\"\u003eApplication Programming Interface (API)\u003c/a\u003e to limit information leakage, and apply PETs such as Trusted Research Environments to protect data sets\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eintegrate re-identification risk into your security and risk management processes\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"test-and-validate\"\u003eTest and validate \u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eBefore going live with a new service, you must thoroughly test to ensure that it works as intended and does not introduce new privacy risks. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should conduct testing throughout the build phases, and repeat it after your service goes live. This is particularly important if any changes are made to the system, data source(s), or when there are significant societal changes that may impact the service.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere possible, you should conduct tests with anonymised or synthetic data. If it’s necessary to test with personal data, make sure you do this in a secure environment with strict limitations on access.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRed teaming exercises may help to probe the service or AI system. Pay particular attention to any:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata that may be exposed which links the protected characteristics as defined in the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance\"\u003eEquality Act 2010\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehealth and location data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata that may relate to vulnerabilities\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/\"\u003eNational Cyber Security Centre\u003c/a\u003e has guidance on protecting personal data, including the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/cyber-assessment-framework\"\u003eCyber Assessment Framework\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"be-transparent-and-give-users-control\"\u003eBe transparent and give users control\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eUsers who are impacted by your service should be able to understand what information you collect, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat it will be used for\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow long you’ll retain it\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow they can manage their privacy settings\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis information should be clearly available at the point of use. Use clear and accessible language in privacy documentation, avoiding jargon and legalistic terms where possible. When interacting with the public, we recommend offering configurable privacy options. A good rule of thumb is to make it as easy to opt-in as it is to opt-out, give people free choices and respect users’ autonomy. You can also review previous \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.bi.team/publications/active-online-choices-designing-to-empower-users-2/\"\u003egovernment research\u003c/a\u003e into how different ways of collecting consent can impact users’ behaviour and enable ‘active’ online choices.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are basic requirements for consent to be legally valid. It must be properly informed, freely given, specific and unambiguous. If you rely on the consent of data subjects, you also need to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprovide an effective and straightforward way for them to withdraw their consent\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etell users what withdrawal means for the service they receive\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe concept of ‘freely given consent’ implies providing a real choice for the data subject. Any element of inappropriate pressure or influence which could affect the outcome of that choice renders the consent invalid. The law takes a certain imbalance between the controller and the data subject into consideration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, in an employer-employee relationship the employee may worry that refusal to consent may have negative consequences for their employment relationship. Similar issues of imbalance arise between people and the state, where there is little or no choice for people when it comes to many public services. For example, there’s no alternative when it comes to seeking welfare benefits, or applying for a passport. Here, consent can only be a valid lawful basis for processing in a few exceptional circumstances.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe also encourage a privacy-by-default approach, where the most privacy-preserving settings are enabled by default unless the user decides to choose otherwise.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTransparency extends beyond privacy notices. You should design processes to ensure users understand how their data is being used at every point. This builds trust and supports informed consent. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should review your service at important points, including milestones and significant updates. This will ensure that you’re still achieving your intended goals and aligning users with your use of data. Even if your service does not change, societal expectations may.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"plan-for-and-respond-to-data-breaches\"\u003ePlan for and respond to data breaches\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eEven with strong safeguards, it’s impossible to guarantee that breaches will never happen. Prepare in advance to ensure you have answers to the following questions:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewho investigates suspected breaches and how?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow can you contain potential breaches and secure data?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow will you inform impacted users of a breach?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat support will you offer to anyone harmed by a breach?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eA well-handled breach can reduce or eliminate harm and preserve public trust, while a poorly handled one may cause lasting damage.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEnsure that your safeguards and processes evolve and adapt to a changing threat landscape. \u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"decommissioning\"\u003eDecommissioning\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must retire all platforms at an appropriate time.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis may be when:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe service is no longer needed\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eyour purpose is better met, or greater public benefit is achieved, with a new service\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe public benefit of the current system is no longer meeting social expectations\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen decommissioning a service, make sure you honour data retention limits, including any data which has been stored or processed by third-party organisations. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere there’s a legal duty or other obligation to retain certain data, ensure this is done securely and with strict access controls, and that confidentiality is protected.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe encourage teams to record, and publish in their internal knowledge bases, any lessons learned about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow privacy risks were managed\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epublic attitudes towards data sharing and AI – ensuring that these findings are aligned with any agreements that were in place with research participants\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"recommended-actions-3\"\u003eRecommended actions\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003einvolve information governance teams early in the project design process – this will help you to comply with privacy and data protection legislation, and plan resources effectively so that support is available for project teams when needed\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003erecord the purpose and benefit to understand why any data collection is necessary and whether it’s balanced against privacy risks, and use this record to ensure your project does not grow beyond its defined scope\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eembed privacy by design and default from the outset – undertake a Data Protection Impact Assessment (\u003cabbr title=\"Data Protection Impact Assessment\"\u003eDPIA\u003c/abbr\u003e) to access and mitigate against data privacy risks\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eadopt data minimisation techniques – ensure that the data you collect and process is the lowest amount required to achieve your purpose\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003efacilitate data subjects’ rights – build in mechanisms for data access and correction, and ensure consent is informed and meaningful\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse PETs where possible, applying techniques such as anonymisation or the use of synthetic data\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eshare data responsibly by having a robust, privacy-preserving governance regime that safeguards:\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003esecurity\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003elawful basis\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eexplicit retention or deletion protocols,\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eprovisions that secure individuals’ privacy and data protection rights as part of sharing agreements and records\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsider the impact of AI – explore additional privacy risks that AI systems may introduce, such as re-identification of individuals in data sets\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eusing public AI tools, such as ChatGPT, can increase the risk of data leakage\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ebe transparent by providing clear privacy notices that tell users exactly how their data is being used and their options, and give users a free choice to configure settings\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eprepare for breaches – develop clear plans and assign responsibilities to investigate and tackle any suspected data breaches\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eplan for decommissioning – create plans for data archival or deletion at an appropriate time, considering how long the data will be needed for the service you’re providing and the life cycle of your project\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eEnvironmental sustainability means thinking about the wider impact of your project on people and the planet, and being mindful about the resources you use every day. It’s important to consider this from the start, as it can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor data and AI projects, acting sustainably means:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eusing only the necessary resources\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprotecting natural resources and using them responsibly\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edesigning systems that last and are easy to maintain\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eSustainability also includes social responsibility. This means supporting inclusion, fairness and human rights in how technologies are designed, manufactured, used and disposed of.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-environmental-sustainability-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat environmental sustainability means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eData and AI can support environmental goals, such as predicting weather patterns or monitoring biodiversity levels. However, developing and training AI models, especially large language models (LLMs), requires the use of critical minerals, energy, water and computing resources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis means that you should consider environmental impact:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eat every level in your organisation – from analysts to senior decision-makers\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eacross the entire life cycle of your tool or project – including when it is decommissioned or handed over to another team\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe complex supply chains of data-driven technologies, and the natural resources required to build them, mean they can have a long-lasting impact on people and the planet. For example, the mining of raw materials to build computing chips and other AI infrastructure. This has a significant environmental cost and impact on the health and wellbeing of workers and affected communities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSetting clear sustainability objectives and using greener software practices will help make sustainability a core part of your project design.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should also consider whether there’s a reasonable trade-off between the benefits of your tool or system and its environmental impact. There may be trade-offs between different ethical principles. For example, the use of a more energy-intensive algorithm that’s also more explainable, or that brings wider benefits and value to the public. Make sure you clearly document when you’ve made decisions about trade-offs, and the governance processes you used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"measuring-monitoring-and-evaluating-environmental-impact\"\u003eMeasuring, monitoring and evaluating environmental impact\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eSustainability reporting for cloud and wider digital services is an evolving area where research and development is ongoing. This means it may be challenging to identify appropriate metrics, and the reliability of reporting may differ across suppliers. The following tools and methods will provide you with a starting point.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBefore you begin building a tool or system, think about:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhether AI is the best technology or tool for the task – there may be alternatives that provide as good, or better, results and require less resource-intensive training and development\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eproject size and complexity – how much data will be processed, the number of end users, bandwidth and latency requirements, prompt efficiency\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esoftware requirements – including model type \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehardware requirements – such as data centre usage or Internet of Things (IoT) devices\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are various environmental factors that you should monitor and manage across the life cycle of your project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eElectricity consumption\u003c/strong\u003e\u003cbr\u003eData centres use large amounts of electricity for running servers and data processing. Some even use fossil fuel-based generators due to a lack of capacity in local grids. Using electricity results in the release of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane and nitrous oxide, which contribute to climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWater consumption\u003c/strong\u003e\u003cbr\u003eFor example, data centres require significant amounts of fresh water for cooling systems and to avoid hardware failure.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eConsumption of raw materials\u003c/strong\u003e\u003cbr\u003eThe mining of raw materials, for example to build computing chips and other AI infrastructure, has a significant environmental cost and impact on the health and wellbeing of workers and affected communities.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv role=\"note\" aria-label=\"Information\" class=\"application-notice info-notice\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eE-waste\u003c/strong\u003e\u003cbr\u003eElectronic waste (e-waste) from discarded electrical devices contains rare earth materials such as neodymium; if not disposed of properly, these materials can contaminate soil and water, and release noxious gases into the atmosphere, posing extremely harmful risks to biodiversity, human health and the environment.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn your project, consider how the following may impact resource consumption:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edata set size – large data sets require more energy to store and process, especially when used to train AI systems, and you should also consider the impact of the resolution or bit rate of the data sets\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edata type – generating or handling high-volume text (for example, training LLMs), video or image data is typically more energy-intensive than other data types because it requires more intensive computing, memory and bandwidth workloads\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edata velocity – high-velocity data (such as real-time streaming) increases compute load\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003earchitecture – using technologies like virtualisation can reduce energy consumption, hardware needs and associated resource demands by allowing data to be accessed and queried without the need for transfer or duplication; adopting modular design can help promote reuse and reduce future resource consumption\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003estorage – data storage has an ongoing carbon footprint, primarily in data centres, due to the continuous generation of heat and use of water and electricity to run them; establishing and running data centres also involves biodiversity loss from land clearing, droughts caused by fresh water extraction, e-waste and pollutants\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emodel type – multi-purpose, generative architectures typically use more resources than task-specific systems; you should always explore different options, including not using AI at all, before choosing a technical approach\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emodel size – LLMs and other generative AI systems generally require more energy and emit more carbon compared to running a single prediction on a trained model\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003elocation – try to run algorithms in locations with higher uses of renewable energy to reduce your carbon footprint\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eyou can use electricity maps to understand the electricity usage and emissions of different regions\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eyou should adhere to any relevant data residency rules if selecting a server location based on energy mix\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etime of day – the source of energy on the grid changes during the day; where it’s viable, you can make carrying out computationally complex processing tasks more environmentally friendly by shifting the time they take place, even by a few hours, to when energy generation is cleaner\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"selecting-metrics\"\u003eSelecting metrics\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should select appropriate metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs) that can be tracked over time. There are several ways of quantifying environmental impact across the development and deployment phases of a project.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCommon metrics include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecarbon footprint (CO2-equivalent emissions)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eenergy consumption (measured kilowatt-hour or kWh)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecompute efficiency (for example, FLOPs per watt – how many calculations a system can perform for every watt of power it uses)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewater consumption (measured in litres)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are some open-source tools that can help to analyse and measure the environmental impact of a data or AI project:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://digitaldecarb.org/data-carbon-ladder/\"\u003eData Carbon Ladder\u003c/a\u003e can provide an estimated data CO2 footprint for your project, highlighting areas to improve to minimise environmental impact – this tool is particularly useful at the project planning stage\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://codecarbon.io/\"\u003eCodeCarbon\u003c/a\u003e is a software package that integrates into your Python codebase; it estimates the amount of CO2 produced by the cloud or personal computing resources used to execute the code\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://mlco2.github.io/impact/\"\u003eML CO2 Impact\u003c/a\u003e is a free machine learning emissions calculator which provides information about the raw carbon emissions produced and the approximate offset carbon emissions of a given project\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/26686\"\u003eCarburacy\u003c/a\u003e is a carbon-aware accuracy measure for evaluating the eco-sustainability of Natural Language Processing (NLP) models\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ecologits.ai/latest/\"\u003eEcoLogits\u003c/a\u003e is a tool that can help to track the energy consumption and environmental impacts of using generative AI models through APIs\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt’s important to note that there are often trade-offs when selecting particular metrics over others, and some impacts will be harder to quantify. For example, carbon emissions may be more easily tracked but neglect a tool’s broader impact, like water usage or impact on local communities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"minimising-environmental-impact\"\u003eMinimising environmental impact\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere’s no one-size-fits-all approach to minimising your environmental impact, but even small actions can make a big difference. Depending on your project, there are many ways to make a positive change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you’re handling or analysing data, you should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eminimise the data you’re collecting and using – collect only the data necessary to meet the research or project objectives\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse data compression and aggregation to reduce storage and bandwidth requirements – for example, compressing data before transmission (using formats like GZIP or Parquet) can help to save bandwidth\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eregularly review whether the data you hold to help reduce its volume – consider whether there’s any redundant, obsolete or trivial (ROT) data that can be safely deleted\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eavoid re-running entire pipelines – use incremental workflows which only re-process new or changed data\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse cloud storage tiers, scaling and right-sizing instances – this can help to optimise data storage allocation by, for example, automatically moving infrequently accessed (‘cold’) data to lower-energy storage\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse narrow prompts for \u003cp\u003euse techniques such as virtualisation to reduce duplication\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edesign modular components for potential reuse in future projects\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you’re building AI or algorithmic tools (including using pre-trained models), you should:\u003cbr\u003e\n- consider reuse for specific tasks – this can help to reduce cost and power consumption, making the technology easier to deploy\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse model or model pruning to remove unused or unnecessary parameters\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eclean up unused resources, such as idle or outdated coding notebooks\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eintroduce early stopping rules to stop training when a model’s performance plateaus – this can prevent redundant training cycles\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003efind out about the environmental credentials of models – if you’re using open-source models, you can find information on
