        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThe use of data and AI is already changing how people live and work. For example, the accessibility of tools such as ChatGPT has started to reshape how we undertake daily tasks. These rapid changes raise important questions about how digital technologies are used, and how they affect society.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSocietal impact refers to the effects that data and AI can have on individuals, communities, social structures and economies. This includes both positive and negative impacts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, adopting chatbots in public sector call centres might reduce costs, boost productivity and allow for faster handling of cases. However, it can also lead to job losses, or create a less personal relationship between government and the public that leaves citizens feeling disempowered.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTaking care to respect other principles such as privacy and fairness can have wider societal impacts, building trust and improving education and health outcomes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEven relatively simple technical solutions can have significant societal impact. For example, an automated form that checks eligibility for a service might unintentionally exclude people if it does not account for different living situations or types of identification. This could stop people from getting the support they need and reduce trust in public services.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-societal-impact-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat societal impact means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo understand how data and AI can impact society, you need to understand the broader social and technical context in which they are used and built.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, the context and mechanisms of data collection can have a significant impact on who is, and is not, represented in a data set. As a result, an entire group of people might be excluded or underrepresented. In the context of government, this could lead to poor or even discriminatory policy decisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBoth complex supply chains and resource usage of data and AI have a significant societal impact. This includes the displacement of local communities, and food and water scarcity in already vulnerable parts of the world. You must consider what knock-on effects your project might have on communities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eProactive public and stakeholder engagement is critical to understand the potential societal impact of a tool or system. Engaging with stakeholders can help to build trust and improve adoption of AI tools and systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should consider:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow data was collected and processed\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewho technology affects and how\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow and where data or a particular technology is used\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow a data-driven system is designed and built\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eData and AI tools can help improve public services and benefit society. However, they also raise societal risks that must be managed, such as:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eunfair treatment – the use of data or AI systems can lead to unequal outcomes, such as people being treated differently based on race, gender or other protected characteristics\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emisinformation and disinformation – AI tools can be used to create misleading or deliberately false content, including text and images, which is then circulated online at scale; this can contribute to the spread of hate speech, in some cases causing widespread distrust and political violence\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003echanges to jobs – automation may reduce demand for some roles and increase the need for new skills; the increased adoption of AI tools has the potential to reshape the world of work, including work becoming less fulfilling\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003echanges to relationships – using technology can change the way people relate to each other, removing opportunities for care, connection and community that can combat loneliness and build trust and community cohesion\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eownership of creative work – the use of generative AI, typically trained on web-scraped data, such as original images and academic articles, raises legal questions about intellectual property and the ownership of content\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003epower imbalances – the information about many AI tools is not transparent or accessible; this can give more control to those who build or use them, and less to those affected, leading to distrust, disaffection and disempowerment\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eadverse impacts on human rights and fundamental freedoms – irresponsibly designed or misused AI technologies can, among other things:\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eharm human dignity\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003edamage physical, psychological and moral integrity\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eundermine freedoms of expression and assembly\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003einfringe on the right to private and family life\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"understanding-stakeholders\"\u003eUnderstanding stakeholders\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo understand your project’s societal impact, identify who could be affected and how. The act of public engagement can help to build trust and improve adoption of new tools and services.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAt the start of your project, you should make sure that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eyour project has a clear purpose\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethere’s a clear public benefit\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eyou’re designing with humans in mind and in a human-centred way\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eEthical use of data and AI means listening to different perspectives and checking that your tools work as intended. Otherwise, you could unintentionally exclude people or cause harm.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should ask:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewho could be negatively or positively affected? \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edo the risks outweigh the expected benefits?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow are the risks and benefits distributed across different groups? \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat might be the long-term consequences?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo better understand the lived experiences of users, it can be helpful to use qualitative and \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/ethnographic-study-qualitative-studies\"\u003eethnographic methods\u003c/a\u003e such as observations, informal conversations or interviews. Think about how different people experience services, including colleagues who will be using the tools.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eConsider:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eage\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edisability\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003egender reassignment\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emarriage and civil partnership\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epregnancy and maternity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erace\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereligion or belief\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esex and sexual orientation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eincome\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eaccess to technology\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eother attributes relevant to your project\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo better understand the views of, or potential impacts on, wider stakeholders and the public, consider proactive stakeholder or public engagement. For a helpful overview, refer to the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/sustainability-1/?modulepage=stakeholder-engagement\"\u003eAlan Turing Institute’s stakeholder engagement overview\u003c/a\u003e or \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://connectedbydata.org/topics/participation\"\u003eresources from Connected by Data\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should factor in ways to empower the public and workers who may be using data and AI tools. To adopt AI safely and effectively, teams should have:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esuitable training and resources\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ea working environment that considers and prioritises broader ‘human’ factors – including cultural shifts, organisational change and skill development\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo learn more, refer to the guidance on \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-human-centred-approach-to-scaling-and-de-risking-ai-tools/the-people-factor-a-human-centred-approach-to-scaling-ai-tools-html\"\u003ea human-centred approach to scaling AI tools\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should continually revisit user needs throughout your project. The Service Manual explains more about \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/start-by-learning-user-needs\"\u003euser needs\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"identifying-harms-and-benefits\"\u003eIdentifying harms and benefits\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eA practical way to identify the harms and benefits of a data or AI project is to bring teams and affected people and communities together to discuss:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe intended and unintended consequences of the system\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat could go wrong\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat can be done to mitigate risks\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eNot all harms and potential impacts are obvious. You should factor in time during the project planning stage to run workshops, following practices such as The \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-model-for-responsible-innovation/the-model-for-responsible-innovation\"\u003eModel for Responsible Innovation\u003c/a\u003e or \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://doteveryone.org.uk/project/consequence-scanning/\"\u003eConsequence Scanning\u003c/a\u003e. The Model for Responsible Innovation is a practical tool created by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) to help teams across the public sector to innovate responsibly with data and AI. You can use the model to run red teaming workshops with teams developing data-driven technology.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHorizon or risk scanning workshops can help to create an open dialogue, so team members, colleagues and external stakeholders can raise concerns and ideas. As part of this scanning, include structured reflection on the team’s perspectival limitations and stakeholder diversity to mitigate blind spots. Often, project teams do not sufficiently reflect the social and demographic characteristics of affected groups. This can limit inclusion of impacted viewpoints and reduce the ability to identify, understand and weigh risks, benefits and trade‑offs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-guide-to-inclusive-social-research-practices/a-guide-to-inclusive-social-research-practices\"\u003ePositionality‑aware\u003c/a\u003e analysis, coupled with meaningful engagement, can surface concerns and opportunities more effectively and equitably. Adopting this reflective and inclusive approach can help to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eidentify risks before they happen\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emake more informed decisions about design and use\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ealign projects more closely with organisational and societal values\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebuild systems that are safer, more trustworthy and more contextually responsive to user needs and interests\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"continuous-monitoring-and-evaluation\"\u003eContinuous monitoring and evaluation\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eUsually, the full effect of a project or tool is not fully known during design and development. This means teams may miss risks or unintended consequences until the system is used in the real world.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should continuously monitor for potentially harmful societal impacts, and actively address them. This includes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eproviding ways for users and other stakeholders to give feedback – such as adding a feedback form to a service or webpage, or running follow-up user research sessions\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emaking adjustments based on user engagement and testing – such as adapting your design or approach when you identify risks\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ebeing transparent about decisions – keep a clear record of what was changed, why, and who was involved; refer to the \u003ca href=\"#transparency-section\"\u003eTransparency\u003c/a\u003e section for more on this\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emonitoring the system post-deployment for any unintended impacts of the system, such as factors relating to workforce engagement or public trust\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eevaluate outcomes based on demographic segments, for example by checking if the tool is affecting groups in unequal ways\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethink about how the introduction of a data-driven tool or approach could inadvertently embed a particular worldview\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ereviewing and evaluating on a continuous basis, and when real-world conditions change – pay attention to the dynamic and changing character of the technology (for example, AI models are regularly updated) and to the shifting conditions of the real-world environments in which systems will be embedded\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsidering independent evaluation – commissioning external evaluation, such as audits, can provide impartial perspectives that can help with building trust\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor more guidance, refer to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://testing-ai-standards.github.io/cross-gov-ai-testing-framework/\"\u003eAI Testing and Assurance Framework for Public Sector\u003c/a\u003e – this covers continuous monitoring and improvement of AI systems post-deployment\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/guidance-on-the-impact-evaluation-of-ai-interventions-html\"\u003eGuidance on the Impact Evaluation of AI Interventions\u003c/a\u003e for best practice in carrying out a robust impact evaluation of programmes and initiatives using AI systems in central government or the delivery of public services\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"recommended-actions-5\"\u003eRecommended actions\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewrite down project objectives in non-technical terms, so that you understand the objectives before jumping to a technical solution\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003efor example, ‘the project seeks to [enhance public safety, reduce waiting times, improve customer experience]’\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einvolve diverse stakeholders in the design and testing process – undertake thorough user research and public engagement, ensuring that you include the views of those likely to be most affected by the project\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethis might include running co-design workshops or focus groups\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ecomplete an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA) – this can help to ensure that the project and its outcomes are fair and do not disadvantage protected groups\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003euse feedback mechanisms, such as surveys and advisory boards, to enable stakeholders to continuously shape project outcomes – this can help to reduce any negative impacts across the project life cycle\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emake sure you have meaningful human control at the right stages – having human oversight of AI systems can help to maintain accountability and correct any erroneous or potentially harmful impacts\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econtinuously evaluate and improve the project to ensure it’s meeting user needs and its intended use, by asking:\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eat the beginning of the project, are we doing the right thing?\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eduring the project, have we designed it well and how can we improve?\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eafter the project, is it still doing the thing we designed it for, and if it’s no longer serving a purpose, is there a process or decommissioning the system with minimal impact on end users?\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eIn the context of data and data-driven technologies, safety refers to themes such as accuracy, security, reliability and robustness. It also covers topics such as the safety of researchers and research participants, and safe personal data collection and management.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the context of AI, safety means ensuring that a system performs as intended across its life cycle, even in unexpected circumstances. This is particularly important in high-risk areas such as healthcare, policing and justice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe scale and criticality of government services means they have the potential to cause widespread harm if they’re not designed with safety in mind.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf data-driven systems are not built safely, they can:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eperform poorly and produce incorrect results\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecause harm to individuals and society\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereduce trust in public services and organisations\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eImportant concepts for data and AI safety are:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eaccuracy – making sure that data is accurate and high quality, and that AI systems perform accurately\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003esecurity – protecting data and AI systems against unauthorised access, tampering and leakage\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ereliability – ensuring that data pipelines and AI systems consistently deliver acceptable and expected results in all expected scenarios across the duration of use and deployment\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003erobustness – designing data infrastructure and AI systems to withstand unexpected inputs, adversarial attacks and failures across the duration of its deployment\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eprotection from harm – data use and AI systems must not cause harm to individuals, society or the planet\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003econtrollability – maintaining human oversight over data and AI systems, including the ability to intervene and align outcomes with societal values\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFind out more about AI safety principles in the Alan Turing Institute’s \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/safety/\"\u003eguidance on AI Safety in Practice\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/understanding-artificial-intelligence-ethics-and-safety\"\u003eUnderstanding artificial intelligence ethics and safety\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"what-safety-means-in-practice\"\u003eWhat safety means in practice\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eSafety considerations can emerge across a project life cycle – from initial research and data collection, to the downstream impacts of a system.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the context of data collection, sharing and use, safety means:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensuring data is only used for lawful purposes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehandling data in a way that protects individuals’ privacy and minimises harm\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensuring data is of high quality\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eusing secure systems for storing and processing data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eapplying appropriate anonymisation techniques\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the context of data-driven tools and AI systems, safety means:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edesigning data-driven systems that work as expected and do not cause harm\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etesting systems to make sure they perform accurately and reliably under unexpected conditions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ekeeping systems secure and protecting them from misuse\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"start-with-safe-research\"\u003eStart with safe research\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eResearch is vital to design a project responsibly and robustly, and make sure that systems and products meet user needs. Research can help you understand fairness issues and build trust.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eResearch and data collection are often essential for improving government services and shaping new projects. But both quantitative and qualitative research can carry risks for participants.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must consider the safety of both researchers and participants before starting a project. You should have safeguards in place and maintain them for as long as needed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eQualitative research can carry risks if not planned carefully. This type of research involves collecting non-numerical data, such as:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einterviews \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003efocus groups\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edirect observations\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe safety of research participants in qualitative research is critical. Participants may be at risk of harm or distress, especially if the research involves sensitive topics. There may also be risks to their physical safety – for example, if taking part causes tension within their community or social group.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"reduce-risks-for-participants\"\u003eReduce risks for participants\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou must take steps to protect research participants. This applies to your team and to any third-party researchers you work with. \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emake sure that participants understand the research and any risks involved \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eonly include participants who give clear, informed consent without pressure or coercion \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eallow participants to withdraw at any time (with exceptions for situations like medical research where participant information is anonymised and aggregated and cannot be removed from the research data set)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eanonymise all data used in reports or analysis \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAnonymising qualitative data can be difficult. Even if names, places or dates are removed, the detail in participants’ stories may still make them identifiable. You should take extra steps to protect their identity. The Service Manual has guidance on \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy\"\u003emanaging user research data and participant privacy\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"reduce-risks-for-researchers\"\u003eReduce risks for researchers\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eSome research projects involve sensitive topics, such as child protection or adult safeguarding. These can be distressing for both researchers and participants. To reduce risk, you should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehighlight any sensitive topics in workshop or interview plans\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eset up a ‘safety check-in’ protocol to support staff after sessions, particularly for one-to-one or lone working\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euse existing ethical guidelines and processes, such as the Service Manual’s guidance on \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/researching-emotionally-sensitive-subjects\"\u003eresearching emotionally sensitive subjects\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn rare cases, researchers may be targeted by participants or others. If this happens, or if the risk is known in advance, put safeguards in place to protect staff.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Government Analysis Function provides \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/\"\u003ea list of resources\u003c/a\u003e related to conducting research and analysis in government.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"safe-data-collection-and-management\"\u003eSafe data collection and management\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are several safety risks related to the collection and management of data, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003epoor data quality – including incomplete data, duplicated data, and insufficient or poor-quality metadata\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edata leakage – the unauthorised exposure of personal or sensitive information\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edata drift – the changes in the statistical properties of real-world data distributions over time, which can affect the performance of machine learning models trained on historical data\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edata poisoning – a malicious act where a hacker compromises data sources during collection and pre-processing by introducing corrupted data\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eData security principles and processes are required the moment you begin collecting data. Limiting the amount and sensitivity of data that you collect reduces the potential for harm if data is exposed. Principles like data minimisation, as covered in the \u003ca href=\"#privacy-section\"\u003ePrivacy\u003c/a\u003e section, are relevant to safety and security.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLoss or theft of personal data can have wide-reaching legal and financial consequences. It can also cause significant psychological harm to people affected. Working directly or indirectly with data in the public sector comes with a duty to protect the personal data you hold about individuals. Refer to the government’s \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services\"\u003epersonal data security principles\u003c/a\u003e when processing and sharing personal data.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you’re working with any third-party suppliers to store, collect or process data, make sure they’re vetted and that they comply with the security requirements of your project. There’s guidance on security measures for AI systems in the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government\"\u003eAI Playbook for the UK Government.\u003c/a\u003e \u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ensure-data-is-fit-for-purpose\"\u003eEnsure data is fit for purpose\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll civil servants have a responsibility to ensure that the data they manage and use is of high quality and fit for purpose. Data quality should be checked and validated across the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework/the-government-data-quality-framework#The-Data-Lifecycle\"\u003edata life cycle\u003c/a\u003e. This includes ensuring data is fit for purpose before, during and after data analysis or model development and deployment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRefer to the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework\"\u003eGovernment Data Quality Framework\u003c/a\u003e for guidance on understanding, documenting and improving data quality, and for information about real public sector case studies. The framework sets out the main dimensions of data quality, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecompleteness\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euniqueness\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsistency\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etimeliness\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003evalidity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eaccuracy\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eMaintaining data quality is a continuous process. You should maintain clear documentation of any known limitations, biases and quality concerns. If using data for analysis and model development, you should conduct ongoing validation of outputs, especially where models are reused or retrained.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTools such as data sheets or data set cards can be helpful in documenting information about data quality. The \u003ca href=\"#transparency-section\"\u003eTransparency\u003c/a\u003e section has more information on this.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"data-and-model-poisoning\"\u003eData and model poisoning\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eData poisoning, otherwise known as AI or model poisoning, is a type of cyberattack that involves hackers modifying or introducing new data points into a training data set.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eData poisoning attacks can be direct or indirect. Direct attacks involve deliberately manipulating a machine learning model to behave in a particular way. Indirect attacks aim to degrade the performance of models more generally. This could include inserting irrelevant or incorrect data into a training set, reducing model accuracy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt can be difficult to determine if and how data poisoning has taken place, particularly when using an AI model from a third-party source. For example, poisoned models may function as expected until triggered by a specific prompt or scenario.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eData poisoning can occur in different ways across the data and AI life cycle, such as:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecollecting and using data from uncontrollable or unreliable sources, like social media or Internet of Things (IoT) devices\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eweak access controls \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emalicious actors modifying training data labels to reflect wrong information\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"a-data-poisoning-example\"\u003eA data poisoning example\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eA company builds a voice assistant that helps users control smart devices. To improve the system, the company invites users to help by transcribing voice recordings.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA competitor finds out about this and deliberately mislabels thousands of recordings. For example, they label recordings of users saying “turn the lights off” as “turn the lights on”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOver time, the system learns the wrong behaviour. After an update, the AI assistant starts turning lights on when users ask for them to be turned off, and vice versa. This leads to a poor user experience and damages the company’s reputation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"the-impact-of-data-poisoning\"\u003eThe impact of data poisoning\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe impacts of an AI model trained or fine-tuned with poisoned data are wide-ranging, including:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esecurity threats to the organisation deploying the model\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebiased or harmful outputs being sent to users \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epoor system performance and accuracy, such as misclassification\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eReducing the risk of data poisoning should include technical safeguards and clear policies for data management.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eExample steps include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eusing encryption and strict access controls to prevent unauthorised access to systems and data sets\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethe Information Commissioner’s Office has \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/security/encryption/\"\u003eguidance on encryption\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eindustry-standard encryption methods and protocols, such as advanced encryption standards (AES 256) and Transport Layer Security/Secure Socket Layer (TLS/SSL), also apply to AI systems, data sets and models\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econducting supply chain checks, as poisoned models often originate from pre-trained models that have been fine-tuned using poisoned or compromised data sources\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eimplementing strong validation techniques to check data set quality and accuracy – methods such as anomaly detection can help to detect abnormal outliers and extreme data points\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emonitoring and auditing systems for signs of unusual behaviour, such as sudden drops in system performance\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"building-safe-ai-systems\"\u003eBuilding safe AI systems\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eAI systems can behave in unexpected ways, especially if they’re designed poorly or deployed without adequate testing. Many AI systems work in complex and unpredictable environments. This makes it harder to build systems that are safe and reliable.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eElements to consider in the context of AI safety include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esafety of data – ensuring that data used for AI model training and AI system operation is accurate, high quality and legally compliant\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethis should include testing data for anomalies, identifying and addressing harmful biases, and documenting information about data sets\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esafety of the AI model – ensuring that the model is technically robust and reliable, and performs accurately even in unexpected conditions\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003econsider testing and measuring model performance on validation data sets against metrics such as accuracy and precision, and fairness metrics\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esafety of the AI system – ensuring that the AI system functions safely and as intended within its wider context, including with users and other systems\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003econtinually monitor for unusual behaviour post-deployment, including any potentially harmful outputs\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should prioritise the technical objectives of accuracy, reliability, security and robustness from the outset. Building an AI system that meets these objectives requires testing, validation and re-assessment throughout its entire life cycle. It also requires maintaining human oversight and control.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou should run rigorous testing to identify potential failure modes for AI systems. This may include using semi-automated techniques, such as using adversarial models to develop prompts, or red teaming exercises, to record how models behave under unexpected scenarios.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf it’s not possible to make the system sufficiently safe for the intended use, even with available mitigations, because of the potential risks or failure modes, you should not use the system to address the problem.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf using off-the-shelf generative AI tools, you will likely need to put additional guardrails in place, such as pre- and post-prompt filters. While no generative AI system can be guaranteed to be entirely safe, these measures, combined with ongoing testing and monitoring, can help reduce risks to an acceptable level.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eConsider adopting the following practices to make AI systems safer and more secure:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ebe transparent – you should document information about models, data sets and system prompts, and make sure operators understand how the system works in different situations\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003edesign for resilience – use backup components for critical functions so that the system can continue operating safely even if one element fails\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eapply least privilege principles – distribute responsibility and prevent any single person from having too much control or access\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ebuild in risk controls – build in ways for the system to slow down or stop if it starts to behave in unexpected or unusual ways\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eestablish multiple system defences – apply multiple safety measures rather than relying on just one, including a human-in-the-loop to review outputs\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003econtinually evaluate security factors – you should continually reassess factors that might impact security, including training data sets, model complexity and supply chains\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFind out more about AI safety and security in the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-cyber-security-code-of-practice/code-of-practice-for-the-cyber-security-of-ai\"\u003eCode of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI\u003c/a\u003e and the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/guidelines-secure-ai-system-development\"\u003eguidelines for secure AI system development\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere’s also guidance in the:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/introduction-to-ai-assurance/introduction-to-ai-assurance\"\u003eIntroduction to AI Assurance\u003c/a\u003e which explores AI assurance techniques\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/responsible-ai-toolkit#:~:text=This%20toolkit%20of%20guidance%20aims,over%20time%20with%20new%20resources.\"\u003eResponsible AI Toolkit\u003c/a\u003e which lists various resources that support the safe and responsible development and deployment of AI systems\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://testing-ai-standards.github.io/cross-gov-ai-testing-framework/\"\u003eAI Testing and Assurance Framework for Public Sector\u003c/a\u003e which sets out a practical approach for testing, evaluation and assurance of AI systems\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html\"\u003eAI Playbook for the UK Government\u003c/a\u003e for information about the security and safety of AI systems\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"recommended-actions-6\"\u003eRecommended actions\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eYour team should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003emake sure researchers and research participants are physically and emotionally safe – consider how a research topic could cause distress or discomfort, and reduce these risks by providing clear information, gaining informed consent, and allowing participants to withdraw at any time\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003ecomply with security requirements and standards – new services, including AI systems, must comply with the government’s \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/\"\u003eSecure by Design principles\u003c/a\u003e which help ensure that systems are secure throughout their life cycle\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eapply data minimisation to limit the potential harms of a data breach – this means processing only the minimum amount of personal data necessary to achieve your purpose\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ekeep all data secure throughout the project, referring to the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services\"\u003epersonal data security principles\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003echeck for issues that could affect data quality, accuracy or reliability, such as data drift or model poisoning, by referring to the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework\"\u003eGovernment Data Quality Framework\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eensure human oversight and have strategies to intervene where necessary, especially in high-risk use cases of AI, so that humans can validate decisions and outputs\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003erun rigorous testing to identify potential failure modes for AI systems \n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003ethis may include using semi-automated techniques, such as using adversarial models to develop prompts, or red teaming exercises\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eif it’s not possible to make the system sufficiently safe for the intended use, you should not use it to address the problem\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euse available resources, including the \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://learn.civilservice.gov.uk/courses/f7Sf3JPkTQiwYgr2qatDEw\"\u003ecourses on risks and ethics on Civil Service Learning\u003c/a\u003e and the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html\"\u003eAI Playbook\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"

        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework/data-and-ai-ethics-framework#further-resources",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThere’s a range of \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/data-ethics-guidance\"\u003edata ethics guidance, standards and frameworks\u003c/a\u003e developed by and for government and public sector bodies. These resources support the responsible use and development of data and data-driven technologies, including AI.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/responsible-ai-toolkit\"\u003eResponsible AI Toolkit\u003c/a\u003e also lists guidance related to deploying AI systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Statistics Authority provides \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/what-we-do/data-ethics/centre-for-applied-data-ethics/guidance-and-support/ethics-guidance-documents/\"\u003eguidance related to applied data ethics\u003c/a\u003e in research and statistics.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere are some other public sector resources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ai-knowledge-hub\"\u003eAI Knowledge Hub\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ai.gov.uk/knowledge-hub/\"\u003eAI Knowledge Hub\u003c/a\u003e brings together guidance and case studies for teams adopting AI technologies in the public sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government\"\u003eAI Playbook for the UK Government\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government\"\u003eAI Playbook\u003c/a\u003e offers guidance on using AI safely, effectively and securely for civil servants and people working in government organisations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-atrs\"\u003eAlgorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (\u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard\"\u003eATRS\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/a\u003e provides a standardised way for public bodies to document information about algorithmic tools used in decision-making processes which impact the public.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"analytical-quality-assurance-book-aqua\"\u003eAnalytical Quality Assurance Book (\u003cabbr title=\"Analytical Quality Assurance Book\"\u003eAQuA\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-aqua-book\"\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Analytical Quality Assurance Book\"\u003eAQuA\u003c/abbr\u003e Book\u003c/a\u003e is a best practice guide for civil servants working with analysis and analytical models.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"data-sharing-governance-framework\"\u003eData Sharing Governance Framework\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-sharing-governance-framework/data-sharing-governance-framework\"\u003eframework\u003c/a\u003e is one of a growing suite of tools which enable better use, reuse and sharing of data across government.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"government-data-quality-framework\"\u003eGovernment Data Quality Framework\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework\"\u003eguidance\u003c/a\u003e sets out principles and practices to assess, communicate and improve the quality of data in government. Linked with this, there’s guidance on \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/implementing-a-data-quality-action-plan\"\u003eimplementing a data quality action plan\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"dstl-biscuit-book--assurance-of-ai-and-autonomous-systems\"\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"Defence Science and Technology Laboratory\"\u003eDstl\u003c/abbr\u003e biscuit book – Assurance of AI and Autonomous Systems\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is a \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/assurance-of-ai-and-autonomous-systems-a-dstl-biscuit-book\"\u003eguide\u003c/a\u003e to understanding and describing the trustworthiness of autonomous systems and associated AI algorithms. It was written by the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (\u003cabbr title=\"Defence Science and Technology Laboratory\"\u003eDstl\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"explaining-decisions-made-with-ai\"\u003eExplaining decisions made with AI\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/explaining-decisions-made-with-artificial-intelligence/\"\u003eguidance\u003c/a\u003e is from the Information Commissioner’s Office and the Alan Turing Institute. It gives organisations practical advice to help explain the processes, services and decisions delivered or assisted by AI, to the individuals affected by them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"five-safes-framework\"\u003eFive Safes framework\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/secure-lab/what-is-the-five-safes-framework/\"\u003eFive Safes framework\u003c/a\u003e is a set of principles which enable data services to provide safe research access to data.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"guidelines-for-ai-procurement\"\u003eGuidelines for AI Procurement\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eUse these \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidelines-for-ai-procurement/guidelines-for-ai-procurement\"\u003eguidelines\u003c/a\u003e when procuring AI-powered solutions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"model-for-responsible-innovation\"\u003eModel for Responsible Innovation \u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-model-for-responsible-innovation/the-model-for-responsible-innovation\"\u003eModel for Responsible Innovation\u003c/a\u003e is a practical tool created by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). It helps teams across the public sector and beyond to innovate responsibly with data and AI. You can use the model to run red teaming workshops with teams developing data-driven technology.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"pets-adoption-guide\"\u003ePETs Adoption Guide\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://cdeiuk.github.io/pets-adoption-guide/adoption-guide/\"\u003ePETs Adoption Guide\u003c/a\u003e provides an interactive flowchart to help decision makers determine which privacy enhancing technologies (PETs) might be useful for their project. The guide is primarily aimed at technical architects and product owners working on projects that involve the sharing or processing of sensitive information.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"portfolio-of-ai-assurance-techniques\"\u003ePortfolio of AI assurance techniques\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/ai-assurance-techniques\"\u003eportfolio of AI assurance techniques\u003c/a\u003e provides a searchable repository of cross-industry AI assurance techniques.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"technology-code-of-practice\"\u003eTechnology Code of Practice\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-technology-code-of-practice\"\u003eTechnology Code of Practice\u003c/a\u003e is a set of criteria to help the government design, build and buy technology.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"uksa-ethics-self-assessment-tool\"\u003eUKSA Ethics Self-Assessment Tool\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca rel=\"external\" href=\"https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/the-authority-board/committees/national-statisticians-advisory-committees-and-panels/national-statisticians-data-ethics-advisory-committee/ethics-self-assessment-tool/#pid-archived-guidance\"\u003eEthics Self-Assessment Tool\u003c/a\u003e developed by the UK Statistics Authority gives researchers an easy-to-use framework to review the ethics of their projects throughout the research cycle.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
    }
  ]
}

        <div class="govspeak"><h2 id="introduction">Introduction</h2>

<p>This framework provides a set of principles and activities to guide the responsible development, procurement and use of data and artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector. It helps public servants understand ethical considerations and how to address these in their work.</p>

<p>Data and AI ethics is about using data and data-driven technologies responsibly, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>respecting privacy</li>
  <li>promoting fairness</li>
  <li>protecting individuals, communities and society from harm</li>
</ul>

<p>This includes ensuring that data is collected, shared and used in appropriate, fair, safe, sustainable and transparent ways.</p>

<p>The framework applies to any project that involves:</p>

<ul>
  <li>data (collection, sharing or use)</li>
  <li>data-driven technologies</li>
  <li>AI</li>
  <li>automated decision-making and algorithmic tools</li>
</ul>

<p>In this guidance, this is what we mean when we refer to ‘data and AI’.</p>

<h3 id="who-this-guidance-is-for">Who this guidance is for</h3>

<p>The framework is for people who work in government and other public sector organisations. It’s mainly written for people who are designing, building, maintaining, using or updating projects that use data and AI.</p>

<p>This may include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>developers</li>
  <li>project managers</li>
  <li>analysts</li>
  <li>statisticians</li>
  <li>policy makers</li>
  <li>commercial or procurement professionals</li>
</ul>

<p>We also encourage anyone who works directly or indirectly with data and AI to read this guidance and apply it to their work. This includes operational staff and anyone helping to produce data-informed insight.</p>

<h3 id="how-to-use-this-guidance">How to use this guidance</h3>

<p>Your team should work through the framework together as you plan, implement and evaluate a project. You should regularly revisit it throughout your project, especially when you make changes to your work or project.</p>

<p>The framework covers a broad range of use cases and challenges that you might encounter. Some projects may be limited to certain aspects – for example, data collection and processing – while others may cover a full AI development life cycle. This means you might find certain parts of this guidance more or less relevant to your project.</p>

<h4 id="data-and-ai-ethics-self-assessment-tool">Data and AI Ethics Self-Assessment Tool</h4>

<p>If your team is working on an AI or data-driven technology project, then as well as reading this guidance you should use the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework">Data and AI Ethics Self-Assessment Tool</a>.</p>

<p>The tool will help you capture information, and share learnings, challenges and progress with colleagues. We recommend that you maintain it along with your other project documentation to record decision making across the life cycle of a project.</p>

<h3 id="why-this-guidance-is-important">Why this guidance is important</h3>

<p>Government guidance needs to address the rapidly evolving ethical challenges and risks posed by data and AI technologies. We’ve updated the previous version of this guidance to meet this need.</p>

<p>The Data and AI Ethics Framework bridges the gap between high-level ethical principles and practical actions. It considers themes such as safety, security and privacy through an ethical lens. It does not replace technical or regulatory guidance in these areas, but instead complements and connects to them.</p>

<p>It complements existing tools, standards and guidance, including the:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html">AI Playbook for the UK Government</a></li>
  <li><a href="https://www.gov.uk/data-ethics-guidance/the-model-for-responsible-innovation">Model for Responsible Innovation</a></li>
  <li><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub">Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (<abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>)</a></li>
</ul>

<p>This guidance does not replace:</p>

<ul>
  <li>existing ethics guidance and tools for statisticians and social researchers, such as the UKSA’s <a rel="external" href="https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/the-authority-board/committees/national-statisticians-advisory-committees-and-panels/national-statisticians-data-ethics-advisory-committee/ethics-self-assessment-tool/">Ethics Self-Assessment Tool</a>
</li>
  <li>bespoke guidance provided by individual departments, devolved administrations or for specific professions</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="principles">Principles</h3>

<p>This is an overview of the main principles everyone should follow when working with data and AI in the public sector. The rest of the guidance explores each principle in more detail.</p>

<h4 id="transparency">Transparency</h4>

<p>Transparency means that information about your project, actions, processes and data are communicated to relevant parties in an understandable, easily accessible and free way. Transparency includes the concept of explainability, which refers to the ability to understand and communicate how a system makes decisions, including how it arrived at an individual decision.</p>

<h4 id="accountability">Accountability</h4>

<p>Accountability means that data and AI projects have appropriate and effective governance, oversight, and routes to challenge decisions in place, where this is necessary. It involves setting clear roles and responsibilities, and being transparent about the system and the processes around it.</p>

<h4 id="fairness">Fairness</h4>

<p>Fairness means avoiding unfair biases and impacts, and addressing accessibility barriers, while actively maximising positive impacts. You should assess data representativeness, bias, and the different potential impacts that can result from data use.</p>

<p>You should mitigate model biases and aim for outputs and decisions generated with the help of automated processes to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>be non-discriminatory</li>
  <li>be just</li>
  <li>respect dignity</li>
  <li>align with the public interest, human rights and democratic values</li>
  <li>comply with the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance">Equality Act 2010</a> and the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities">Public Sector Equality Duty (<abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr>)</a>
</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="privacy">Privacy</h4>

<p>Privacy means that personal data is respected and handled responsibly, ensuring it’s used only for intended purposes with an appropriate legal basis. It also means adhering to UK data protection regulation, including principles of data minimisation, purpose limitation and informed consent.</p>

<h4 id="safety">Safety</h4>

<p>Safety refers to the use of data or development of a system without causing harm to people, organisations, wider social institutions or the environment. Data-driven systems such as AI should be robust, secure and safe at every stage of their life cycle. This means ensuring that they operate properly and reliably, without causing unnecessary safety or security risks.</p>

<h4 id="societal-impact">Societal impact</h4>

<p>Societal impact is about how the development and use of data and data-driven technologies impact wider society. For example, by helping to solve societal challenges and deliver public good.</p>

<h4 id="environmental-sustainability">Environmental sustainability</h4>

<p>Sustainability calls for responsible design and use of data and AI that minimises environmental impact, and supports long-term wellbeing for people and the planet. This means considering biospheric consequences when scoping potential AI and data projects, and building tools and systems that are robust and energy efficient. Biospheric consequences are the effects a project can have not only on the planet’s ecosystems but also its climate and the entire biosphere.</p>

<h3 id="trade-offs">Trade-offs</h3>

<p>There may be instances where you find that 2 or more of the ethical principles are in tension with one another. For example, using more demographic information may help to identify biases and promote fairness, but this may come at the expense of an individual’s privacy. Here, you might need to consider trade-offs. Ethical trade-offs are inherently complex and you must treat them with care.</p>

<p>Here are some approaches which can help you establish suitable trade-offs:</p>

<ul>
  <li>include stakeholder perspectives by engaging with affected communities to understand values and impacts</li>
  <li>consult legal and human rights frameworks to ensure that decisions align with national and international standards</li>
  <li>balance proportionality and necessity</li>
  <li>ensure meaningful and inclusive deliberation</li>
  <li>establish mechanisms to monitor outcomes, and adjust if necessary</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="transparency-section">Transparency</h2>

<p>Transparency is foundational to all other ethical principles. Being transparent allows for scrutiny of actions, decisions and processes. It cultivates accountability and can help to build trust in the use of data and technology. </p>

<p>Explainability applies specifically to AI systems and the ability to describe how a system arrives at a given output or decision. For example, this could include explaining what factors led to a benefit application being granted or denied. Explainability can help to build trust by making it easier to understand decision-making processes, and easier to identify risks, inaccuracies and harms. </p>

<p>A lack of transparency might lead to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>solutions being designed suboptimally – at worst leading to harmful outcomes</li>
  <li>insufficient accountability and no clear ways to appeal decisions of automated systems – which may result in public distrust</li>
</ul>

<p>The first data protection principle in the <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-and-the-eu/data-protection-and-the-eu-in-detail/the-uk-gdpr/">UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK <abbr title="General Data Protection Regulation">GDPR</abbr>)</a> is that of ‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’. In the context of data protection, transparent processing is about being clear, open and honest with people from the start about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>who you are</li>
  <li>how and why you use someone’s personal information</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="what-transparency-means-in-practice">What transparency means in practice</h3>

<p>It can be helpful to think about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>why you’re being transparent</li>
  <li>what you’re being transparent about</li>
  <li>to whom you’re being transparent</li>
</ul>

<p>For why you’re being transparent, consider these questions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>are you following a particular mandate or requirement to be transparent? </li>
  <li>are you trying to address topics such as safety, trust, accountability, internal or external scrutiny, reproducibility, transferability or robustness​?</li>
  <li>what are the potential consequences of not being transparent?​</li>
  <li>how will your organisation balance the resources required to make material transparent with other competing operational priorities?</li>
</ul>

<p>For what you’re being transparent about, consider:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the tools you’re using – for example, for data analysis or automated processes – and explaining the process or context for how you’re using them</li>
  <li>publishing open data or source code, where this is safe and complies with internal governance</li>
  <li>explaining the factors that influence a system’s output</li>
  <li>providing contact details to get in touch with your team</li>
</ul>

<p>In terms of who you’re aiming to be transparent to, consider:</p>

<ul>
  <li>internal transparency within your organisation – for example, record-keeping for handover and continuity purposes</li>
  <li>cross-organisational transparency – for example, sharing case studies with other government departments</li>
  <li>transparency as part of oversight requirements – for example, being transparent to regulators, auditors or evaluators</li>
  <li>transparency with directly affected individuals or defined groups – for example, explaining algorithm-assisted decision making</li>
  <li>public transparency – for example, publishing information about a project on <a rel="external" href="http://gov.uk">GOV.UK</a>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Depending on who you’re trying to be transparent to, you should engage with these people and organisations. Ask them what type and level of transparency would be most meaningful and useful to them. </p>

<p>This might involve:</p>

<ul>
  <li>talking to users about what level of explainability is useful</li>
  <li>talking to civil society about what they need to know to effectively hold you to account</li>
  <li>talking to researchers about what information would help them evaluate the system</li>
  <li>talking to other teams in government about what information they would like about what you’re doing</li>
</ul>

<p>These considerations will help you identify the right content and level of transparency to use in each specific case, across relevant stakeholder groups. As an example, you might be the owner of a data set that others might benefit from, and which does not contain personal data. You might consider publishing it openly on <a rel="external" href="http://data.gov.uk">data.gov.uk</a>. However, where personal data is concerned, you may have to provide transparency information in response to a data subject access request via official channels.</p>

<p>As another example, if you want to ensure a smooth handover of an in-house AI system, you might choose to record and share its technical details and source code with colleagues. This will ensure it remains safe, functional and easy to maintain. Or, if you’re generating explanations of a system’s outcome to affected parties, you may adapt transparency information to include simple, non-technical and user-accessible explanations where possible.</p>

<h3 id="transparency-in-the-context-of-data">Transparency in the context of data</h3>

<p>Data transparency is about communicating:</p>

<ul>
  <li>where the data comes from</li>
  <li>how the data is collected, cleaned, used, stored, shared, analysed and interpreted</li>
  <li>the limitations of the data</li>
  <li>how you’ve complied with applicable laws – for example, data protection and intellectual property law</li>
</ul>

<p>This applies to the data itself, but also to metadata (such as file format or author) and paradata (data about the data collection process itself). </p>

<p>Being transparent about data can involve the following elements.</p>

<h4 id="open-data">Open data</h4>

<p>Making data openly available can support trust and transparency by allowing others to replicate and scrutinise published results. If data is non-sensitive, non-personal, and if data sharing agreements with the supplier allow it, you should make the data open and assign it a <a rel="external" href="https://www.doi.org/">digital object identifier (<abbr title="digital object identifier">DOI</abbr>)</a>.</p>

<p>You can publish government data sets on <a rel="external" href="http://data.gov.uk">data.gov.uk</a>, following the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-data-charter">Open Data Charter</a>.</p>

<h4 id="documentation-about-the-provenance-collection-or-generation-of-data">Documentation about the provenance (collection or generation) of data</h4>

<p>If you’re collecting or generating data, it’s important to be open about why, what and how (by which methods) data is being collected.</p>

<h4 id="documentation-about-any-pre-processing-to-address-limitations-of-the-data">Documentation about any pre-processing to address limitations of the data</h4>

<p>Discuss what pre-processing steps you’ve taken to ensure adequate data quality. Disclose any limitations of the data, such as quality issues, missing or incomplete data, gaps in representativeness, or known errors.</p>

<h4 id="documentation-about-how-the-data-is-used-in-a-specific-project">Documentation about how the data is used in a specific project </h4>

<p>When using data in a specific project, clearly communicate the problem domain, user need, project aims and value to relevant stakeholders. When starting data analysis, you should be able to clearly explain the purpose and methodology of your analysis.</p>

<h4 id="documentation-about-data-sharing-and-access">Documentation about data sharing and access</h4>

<p>Be open about who has access to the data, what data sharing agreements are in place, and what the conditions for reuse are, such as licensing.</p>

<h4 id="data-protection-related-transparency">Data protection-related transparency</h4>

<p>Where personal data is being processed, you must comply with relevant laws: You need to carry out a <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/">Data Protection Impact Assessment (<abbr title="Data Protection Impact Assessment">DPIA</abbr>)</a> before you process personal data when the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. It’s good practice to publish your completed <abbr title="Data Protection Impact Assessment">DPIA</abbr> to demonstrate that you’re taking the appropriate precautions to protect personal data and ensure your system is fair.</p>

<p>When processing personal data, you must provide a privacy notice that is easy to locate and explains in clear, accessible language:</p>

<ul>
  <li>why you need the data</li>
  <li>how long you’ll keep the data</li>
  <li>whether you’ll share the data with others</li>
  <li>how people can exercise their rights or raise complaints</li>
</ul>

<p>You should also explain the safeguards that achieve effective <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/">data minimisation</a>, such as anonymisation or pseudonymisation, in plain language.</p>

<p>Concepts such as data sheets or data set cards can be helpful in recording some of this information. Good examples include <a rel="external" href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.09010">data sheets for data sets</a> and variations of data set cards that have been developed based on this approach, such as <a rel="external" href="https://github.com/PAIR-code/datacardsplaybook/blob/main/templates/DataCardsExtendedTemplate.pdf">Google’s data cards</a>.</p>

<p>For more information, refer to the <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/">UK <abbr title="General Data Protection Regulation">GDPR</abbr> guidance and resources</a> on the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) website.</p>

<h4 id="fairness-related-transparency">Fairness-related transparency</h4>

<p>You must comply with the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities/public-sector-equality-duty-guidance-for-public-authorities">Public Sector Equality Duty</a> and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance">Equality Act 2010</a>. This means you need to carefully consider and document the equality impact of processing <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/personal-information-what-is-it/what-is-personal-data/what-is-personal-data/">personal data</a> where it can be used to identify individuals as having a protected characteristic. This document is often referred to as an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA). For more information, consult the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed">EHRC guidance on the Public Sector Equality Duty</a>.</p>

<p>It’s good practice to publish your EIA. This will demonstrate that you’ve considered the potential equality implications (both positive and negative) of processing data that relates to any protected characteristics. Publishing your completed <abbr title="Data Protection Impact Assessment">DPIA</abbr> and EIA will build trust in your use of data and data-driven technologies.</p>

<h3 id="transparency-in-the-context-of-ai-and-algorithmic-tools">Transparency in the context of AI and algorithmic tools</h3>

<p>Ensuring transparency and explainability can be complex in the context of AI, algorithmic and automated systems. Transparency can be limited by ‘black box’ algorithms or proprietary commercial tools. Explainability may not be possible for certain forms of machine learning, or may only be achievable at the cost of performance.</p>

<p>To be transparent in the context of AI and automated systems, you should consider the following concepts.</p>

<h4 id="technical-transparency">Technical transparency </h4>

<p>This is information about the technical operation of the AI system, such as the code used to create the algorithms and the underlying data sets used to train the model.</p>

<h4 id="process-transparency">Process transparency </h4>

<p>This is information about the design, development and deployment decisions and practices behind your AI solutions, and the mechanisms used to demonstrate that the solution is responsible and trustworthy. This may also include an audit log of the prompts and outputs generated by AI systems.</p>

<p>To enable process-based transparency, you should have the following in place:</p>

<ul>
  <li>robust reporting mechanisms</li>
  <li>process-centred governance frameworks</li>
  <li>AI assurance techniques</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="outcome-based-transparency-and-explainability">Outcome-based transparency and explainability </h4>

<p>This means the ability to clarify to any person who is using or impacted by a service that uses AI, how the solution works, and which factors influence its decision making and outputs. This includes individual-level explanations of decisions, where this is requested. It can also include aggregate statistics about outcomes that can be used to monitor fairness.</p>

<h4 id="explainability-in-practice">Explainability in practice</h4>

<p>For certain types of machine learning models, such as deep learning or large language models (LLMs), it can be impossible to fully explain the logic behind an output or decision due to their complex, ‘black box’ nature. For example, LLMs may <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government">hallucinate</a> (where LLMs generate plausible but factually incorrect information) for unexpected reasons. The size and complexity of these models may make it difficult or impossible to identify a determinate causal chain for why this has happened.</p>

<p>You should assess the degree of explainability that’s necessary for your project given its specific domain context and use case. Do this before making technical or architectural decisions about the type of algorithmic techniques you’ll employ in model development. For instance, in high-impact contexts such as social care or criminal justice, you might need a higher level of explainability to ensure fairness and comply with applicable regulation. Considering explainability needs will help you avoid investing in inappropriate technology.</p>

<p>In other cases, where it’s impossible to understand or interpret the rationale behind the outputs of the model, consider alternative methods of explainability such as visualisation techniques or counterfactual explanations. The ICO has guidance on <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/explaining-decisions-made-with-artificial-intelligence/">explaining decisions made with AI</a>.</p>

<h4 id="using-the-algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard">Using the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard</h4>

<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub">Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (<abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>)</a> establishes a standardised way for public sector organisations to publish information about how and why they’re using algorithmic tools.</p>

<p>All central government departments and arm’s length bodies that provide public or frontline services, or routinely interact with the general public, <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-mandatory-scope-and-exemptions-policy/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-atrs-mandatory-scope-and-exemptions-policy">must use the <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr></a>. This involves documenting information about any algorithmic tools used in decision-making processes, and making this clearly accessible to the public.</p>

<p>We also recommend the <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr> to other public sector bodies, such as local government, even if they’re not currently mandated to use it.</p>

<p>Even where a tool does not strictly fall within scope of the <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>, we recommend <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub">publishing an <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr> record</a>.</p>

<h4 id="if-youre-using-a-third-party-supplier">If you’re using a third-party supplier</h4>

<p>Vendors of AI systems must be able to clearly explain:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the steps they take to build tools</li>
  <li>the logic and assumptions built into their tools</li>
  <li>how their tools generate outputs</li>
</ul>

<p>This explanation should include information about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the data used to train the AI model </li>
  <li>the function of the AI models</li>
  <li>the system’s intended purpose</li>
  <li>the steps they’ve taken to mitigate risks</li>
</ul>

<p>Before entering into a contract, consider asking your supplier:</p>

<ul>
  <li>how they engaged with users and affected communities across the development life cycle</li>
  <li>how they identified, evaluated and mitigated risks</li>
  <li>what the source of the data is</li>
  <li>how the data sets were created</li>
  <li>what data the model has been trained on</li>
  <li>if training data sets are sufficiently representative to facilitate fair performance</li>
  <li>where third-party data has been used to train the AI, if the organisation has a valid and lawful basis for processing</li>
  <li>if there are any known biases in the data or the trained model</li>
  <li>how accurate the system is</li>
  <li>if the system has been tested for differential performance on relevant demographic groups</li>
  <li>if the system is based on an LLM, what the observed rate of hallucinations is, and under what conditions they normally occur</li>
  <li>what benchmarks or other modes of model assessment and evaluation have been used to measure safety, reliability, robustness, performance, privacy preservation, toxicity and bias</li>
  <li>if there are any issues likely to affect quality</li>
</ul>

<p>You should update the answers to these questions when significant changes are made to data sets, models, APIs or other relevant components that you’re procuring.</p>

<p>For further guidance on procuring AI systems, refer to the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government">AI Playbook</a> and the <a rel="external" href="https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning">Responsibly buying AI guide for councils in England</a>.</p>

<p>You should consider any tools you’re procuring from a third party which are intended to be used in decision-making processes. These tools might fall within the scope of the mandatory requirement to use the <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>. At the stage, it’s helpful to ensure that the supplier is providing you with all the required transparency information requested in the <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>.</p>

<p>You can also check the <a rel="external" href="https://senseaboutscience.org/responsible-handover-of-ai/">Responsible Handover Framework</a> to identify the information needed for a successful AI system handover from supplier to buyer.</p>
