<h3 id="recommended-actions">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should: </p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>explain the what, how and why of your project in plain language to a non-expert audience; if you cannot articulate how the use of data or AI solves a defined problem, you should consider alternative solutions</p>
  </li>
  <li>maintain detailed records of the project – include the decisions that were made in its design, for example:</li>
  <li>how the project delivers positive social outcomes for the public</li>
  <li>what the user need is that it tries to address</li>
  <li>who the senior responsible owner of the project is</li>
  <li>how a relationship with a third-party supplier was set up </li>
  <li>
    <p>your EIA and <abbr title="Data Protection Impact Assessment">DPIA</abbr></p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>make information publicly available – consider where you can make information about a project or tool publicly accessible, such as on GitHub, in blogs, on <a rel="external" href="http://gov.uk">GOV.UK</a> or on your organisation’s webpage</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use the <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr> if your organisation is within mandatory scope, and consider publishing an <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr> record even if your organisation is not in mandatory scope</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>give appropriate disclosure when AI has been used to produce an output – this concerns both internal and external uses of AI</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>maintain detailed records of all data sources used, including collection methods, licenses and pre-processing steps</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>publish DPIAs and EIAs where possible – refer to the <a href="#fairness-section">Fairness</a> and <a href="#privacy-section">Privacy</a> sections for more information</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>maintain detailed records of all the design decisions and assumptions that went into the development of a solution</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>create and regularly update assurance documentation that explains the model’s purpose, performance limitations and intended use cases – this might include model cards or data set cards</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>if possible, publish your source code openly – for example, on GitHub</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>build algorithmic tools with explainability in mind – consider how important explainability is for the intended use case, and the degree of explainability that would meet domain-specific expectations and regulation</p>
  </li>
  <li>use technical methods for assessing the interpretability of machine learning models – you should have a good working understanding of their limitations:</li>
  <li>common explainability techniques such as <a rel="external" href="https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)</a> and <a rel="external" href="https://c3.ai/glossary/data-science/lime-local-interpretable-model-agnostic-explanations/">LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations)</a> may be helpful in some cases, but may be ineffective for, and inapplicable to, LLMs and generative AI systems</li>
  <li>consult technical experts and state-of-the-art research when choosing appropriate explainability methods</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="accountability-section">Accountability</h2>

<p>Accountability involves setting clear roles and responsibilities and being transparent about decisions. It means that people and organisations are responsible for the data they collect, use and share, and for the technology they build. It also means that if something goes wrong and a system or process harms someone, this can be raised and fixed.</p>

<p>Being accountable helps keep people safe, and ensures that data and AI is used fairly and responsibly. A lack of accountability or failure to uphold ethical standards can result in serious consequences, including:
- unaddressed harm to people, such as unfair decisions
- harm to public services
- legal risks and repercussions
- regulatory action
- reputational damage and a loss of trust in organisations</p>

<h3 id="what-accountability-means-in-practice">What accountability means in practice</h3>

<p>You should take the following steps to establish and support accountability across a data or AI project.</p>

<h4 id="set-clear-roles-and-responsibilities">Set clear roles and responsibilities</h4>

<p>You need strong oversight and clear responsibilities to ensure accountability across the life cycle of your data or AI project. You must set out who is responsible at each stage of the project.</p>

<p>This includes naming:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner">senior responsible owners (SROs)</a> – as the primary risk owners for the project, they ensure a real policy or business need is being addressed, engage with stakeholders and assure ongoing viability</li>
  <li>data owners – data sets must have named data owners accountable for quality, access controls and life cycle governance</li>
  <li>data stewards – they should be responsible for metadata and day-to-day quality controls</li>
  <li>data custodians – they should be responsible for capturing, storing and disposing of data in line with the data owner’s requirements</li>
  <li>AI asset owners – they should be responsible for AI outputs, including model predictions and any generated data</li>
</ul>

<p>For project governance to be effective, it’s essential that the people accountable have appropriate technical expertise and knowledge, and authority, to implement necessary changes. This is especially important for complex projects or those involving multiple suppliers, which is often the case with data and AI projects.</p>

<p>For more information, refer to the:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual">Service Manual</a> – which explains how to build a digital and data team</li>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://ddat-capability-framework.service.gov.uk/#it-operations-job-family">Government Digital and Data Profession Capability Framework</a> – which outlines the skills needed for any digital and data role</li>
  <li>guidance on <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner/the-role-of-the-senior-responsible-owner">the role of the SRO</a>
</li>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/project-delivery-functional-standard">Government Project Delivery Functional Standard</a> – which sets expectations for the management of government projects</li>
  <li>guidance on <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-shared-data-assets-and-data-ownership-in-government/data-ownership-in-government-html">Data Ownership in Government</a> – which sets out a data ownership model that formalises the roles of the people in government responsible for managing data throughout its life cycle</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="traceability-and-auditability">Traceability and auditability</h4>

<p>Your project team should keep clear records to show how your data or AI system was designed, developed and used, who made a decision and the evidence they used. This will make your project accessible for audit, oversight and review by appropriate parties. It will help others check that your work is trustworthy, and that it meets legal and ethical standards.</p>

<p>For any project that uses data, your team must:</p>

<ul>
  <li>name an SRO and data owner for the data</li>
  <li>establish who is responsible for each component of the project, including third-party vendors</li>
  <li>document lawful use and purpose of processing, including legal basis and a recording of processing activities</li>
  <li>register new data assets – either via organisational data catalogues, or cross-departmentally by designating <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/essential-shared-data-assets-and-data-ownership-in-government/essential-shared-data-assets-esdas-guidance-for-departments-html">Essential Shared Data Assets (ESDAs)</a>
</li>
  <li>record and retain audit trails of who has access to the data and why</li>
  <li>record all important decisions and maintain a process log with evidence of responsible data practices</li>
  <li>provide routes for people to raise concerns, complaints or request corrections</li>
</ul>

<p>To ensure AI and algorithmic systems can be audited or reviewed, your team must:
- record who is responsible for each part of the system, including suppliers
- keep information about where the data came from and how it was used – from data collection and preparation, to training, testing and use
- record decisions made during project design, model deployment and system deployment processes
- keep clear records that show how the system was designed, developed, tested and implemented</p>

<p>This information should be easy to find and understandable to a range of stakeholders. For example, a data set factsheet can help explain how data was handled. The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-template">Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (<abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>)</a> also provides a template for public sector organisations to document and share information about how and why they’re using algorithmic tools.</p>

<p>If you’re building an AI system, you should take steps to ensure that the system is explainable. For example, you can explain why a model or algorithmic tool has produced a particular outcome. There are some cases where it can be difficult to trace the inputs and outputs of AI systems, such as large language models (LLMs). The <a href="#transparency-section">Transparency</a> section has more information on explainability.</p>

<h4 id="establish-feedback-mechanisms">Establish feedback mechanisms</h4>

<p>Upholding accountability means ensuring that people affected by the use of a data or AI system can:</p>

<ul>
  <li>understand how decisions were made – this may include data sources, decision-making criteria and logic</li>
  <li>provide feedback</li>
  <li>contest outcomes that are incorrect</li>
  <li>seek redress if they‘ve been affected by erroneous or unjust outcomes – for example, by asking for the decision to be reviewed or corrected, especially in the case of automated decision making</li>
</ul>

<p>You should create a clear mechanism for monitoring the ongoing use of your data or AI project. This involves evaluating how it’s used, and providing a feedback loop where users and operators can identify issues and send them back to the development team.</p>

<p>You should also set up a clear way of handling and responding to feedback, complaints and appeals.</p>

<p>Examples of feedback mechanisms might include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>surveys and feedback forms</li>
  <li>reporting mechanisms integrated into the tool or service</li>
  <li>stakeholder workshops</li>
</ul>

<p>Where appropriate, you should engage with civil society organisations for guidance on how to design and integrate feedback and redress mechanisms for your AI project or system.</p>

<h4 id="maintain-human-oversight">Maintain human oversight</h4>

<p>People must be able to monitor and influence how systems work, even when the system is partially or fully automated. People should remain responsible for the decisions they make when these are supported or informed by an AI system.</p>

<p>If your system includes automated processing, make sure there’s appropriate human oversight. This includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>recording how much of the process is automated and how much is controlled by people</li>
  <li>naming the roles and people responsible for oversight and for managing risks</li>
  <li>avoiding fully automated decisions where the outcome could significantly affect individuals or groups, and making sure a person makes the final decision in these cases</li>
  <li>if using LLM tools, ensuring someone is verifying outputs for incorrect information and potential biases</li>
</ul>

<p>In some AI use cases, automated decision making can be difficult to avoid. For example, it would typically be impossible for humans to review every conversational output of an LLM-based chatbot. Here you should weigh the risks of incorrect or harmful outputs and resulting negative impacts against the benefits of using the system.</p>

<p>In some cases, where the risks of potential harm and incorrect outputs are high, the right choice might be to not use the system at all. In other cases, you may want to put risk mitigations in place – for example, providing easy access to human agents if a chatbot malfunctions or is unable to help users.</p>

<p><strong>If your project uses personal data</strong>, you must meet your legal duties under the <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-and-the-eu/data-protection-and-the-eu-in-detail/the-uk-gdpr/">UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK <abbr title="General Data Protection Regulation">GDPR</abbr>)</a>. This includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>being responsible for how personal data is used</li>
  <li>showing how you meet the data protection principles</li>
  <li>completing and documenting <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/">Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)</a>
</li>
  <li>fulfilling transparency obligations – including the publication of privacy notices or fair processing notices</li>
  <li>enabling people to exercise their data protection rights</li>
</ul>

<p>Your organisation’s data protection officer (DPO) or information assurance team should be able to advise on your data protection obligations.</p>

<h4 id="accountability-if-youre-using-a-third-party-supplier">Accountability if you’re using a third party supplier</h4>

<p>If you buy a data-driven or AI system from a supplier, you must:</p>

<ul>
  <li>make sure the supplier understands their responsibilities</li>
  <li>agree what risks they must manage</li>
  <li>ask them to share information about how the system works</li>
</ul>

<p>As a baseline, make sure that any supplier maintains the same standards as would be expected from you if the system was developed internally. This applies to data governance, performance evaluation, data minimisation and legal accountability.</p>

<p>You should include the following responsibilities in the contract:</p>

<ul>
  <li>product liability – suppliers may be liable if the system causes harm because it gives unsafe outcomes or fails</li>
  <li>data liability – if the system breaks data protection or other applicable law or misuses data</li>
  <li>algorithmic harm – if the system breaks equality law for discriminatory, biased or unfair outcomes, particularly in public services (such as social welfare or policing)</li>
  <li>security liability – liability for damage caused by insufficient security measures or third-party manipulation</li>
  <li>failure to meet contract terms – including penalties, clawback clauses and potential contract termination</li>
  <li>insurance – you can ask suppliers to have insurance that covers harm caused by AI</li>
</ul>

<p>For more guidance on procuring AI technologies, refer to the:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://www.crowncommercial.gov.uk/downloadable-resource/request/67557/buyers-guidance-supporting-the-procurement-of-artificial-intelligence-via-ccs-agreements">Buyer’s guidance on AI procurement</a> </li>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidelines-for-ai-procurement">Guidelines for AI procurement</a> </li>
  <li><a rel="external" href="https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning">Responsibly buying AI guidance</a></li>
</ul>

<p>Ultimately, it’s important to keep in mind that the public body remains responsible for all data and algorithm-assisted decisions or outputs, and their impacts.</p>

<h3 id="recommended-actions-1">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>nominate an SRO, typically a senior decision maker, to be accountable for the project</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>talk to your organisation’s DPO and ensure they have the necessary information, tools and authority to govern the project</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>establish mechanisms for independent reviews of your project to review and challenge decisions relating to data and AI systems, where appropriate</p>
  </li>
  <li>clarify legal responsibilities across the data and AI supply chain, ensuring that all parties involved in the data and AI project life cycle – from vendors and technical teams to system users – are acting lawfully and understand their respective legal obligations
    <ul>
      <li>if you’re buying a system commercially, define detailed responsibilities and liability contractually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>publish information that’s accessible to technical and non-technical stakeholders, and explains:
    <ul>
      <li>how your AI system works (including its purpose, data sources and decision logic) </li>
      <li>how the actions and decisions you’ve taken across the entire AI project life cycle have ensured that it’s ethical, lawful and trustworthy</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>have mechanisms in place for users to provide feedback, such as reporting errors or contesting decisions that might be inaccurate or harmful</p>
  </li>
  <li>establish a human-in-the-loop process to oversee and validate outputs and decisions where AI is used in risky or high-impact situations – this person or team should be able to identify risks and intervene, where appropriate</li>
</ul>

<p>identify who is responsible for the outputs and decisions made by the AI systems you use, and assume responsibility if this is not clear – this includes interactions with LLM-based tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot</p>

<h2 id="fairness-section">Fairness</h2>

<p>Fairness is a diverse concept. It concerns both the way people are treated and described, and how opportunities and resources are distributed in society. Fairness is deeply rooted in our cultural, moral and political practices, and you should regard it as a good in its own right. </p>

<p>Unfairness undermines social and economic opportunity and creates power imbalances. Inequality can undermine the legitimacy of government and erode trust. </p>

<p>Unfairness in your project may result in:</p>

<ul>
  <li>unlawful discrimination and other conduct prohibited in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance">Equality Act 2010</a>
</li>
  <li>growing inequalities and community tensions</li>
  <li>regulatory, reputational and legal risk</li>
</ul>

<p>Fairness in data and AI involves a combination of social, technological and legal concerns to determine whether people and organisations are treated justly, without systemic advantage or disadvantage.</p>

<p>The government’s collection and use of data and implementation of AI systems have wide-reaching impacts on society. Each time a data point is collected or an algorithm deployed, it can have the potential to widen or close gaps in opportunity, representation and resources.</p>

<h3 id="equality-and-inclusion">Equality and inclusion</h3>

<p>Equality and inclusion are fundamental ethical principles for fairness. Equality is about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>ensuring that all people have equality of opportunity</li>
  <li>exercising government functions in a way that’s designed to reduce inequitable outcomes stemming from socio-economic disadvantage</li>
</ul>

<p>You must take care when ensuring equality in your project. Avoid any form of positive discrimination, as this is prohibited. Instead, take positive action such as targeted training and learning more about <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/positive-action-in-the-workplace-guidance-for-employers/positive-action-in-the-workplace">positive action in the workplace</a>.</p>

<p>Inclusion is about ensuring that all groups can use and benefit from your project, accommodating for the needs of different physical and mental abilities and different contextual and cultural needs.</p>

<h3 id="what-fairness-means-in-practice">What fairness means in practice</h3>

<p>Fairness considerations are critical across the life cycle of your project – from initial decisions about what data to collect and how, to the impacts of your project years after deployment.</p>

<p>To understand what fairness means in your project, first determine what aspects of fairness are most relevant to your project. For example:</p>

<ul>
  <li>if your project involves classifying events or objects – such as flagging fraudulent claims – the most relevant interpretation of fairness may be equal error rates between groups</li>
  <li>if your system provides access to a public service or type of benefit – such as access to government grants for research – proportional access may be more important</li>
</ul>

<p>You must understand and comply with your legal obligations and duties. Refer to the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed">Public Sector Equality Duty (<abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr>)</a> and the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance">Equality Act 2010</a>. The <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr> is made of a general duty across Britain, with specific duties that vary between England, Wales and Scotland. There’s guidance for public sector bodies on the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/new-guidance-ai-and-equality-available-public-sector-bodies?return-url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.equalityhumanrights.com%2Fsearch%3Fkeys%3DAi%2Bguidance"><abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr> and AI</a> and a <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/how-consider-equality-policy-making-10-step-guide-public-bodies-england">10-step guide</a> on how to deliver an Equality Impact Assessment.</p>

<div class="call-to-action">
  <h4 id="proxies">Proxies</h4>

  <p>Proxies are data points that are strongly correlated to other characteristics. For example, postcodes might be strongly correlated with age and race. While use of proxies is, in many instances, lawful, it’s essential to review data sets and models for proxies that may be introducing bias.</p>

  <p>This especially applies to bias against <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/equality/equality-act-2010/protected-characteristics">protected characteristics</a> such as:</p>

  <ul>
    <li>age</li>
    <li>disability</li>
    <li>gender reassignment</li>
    <li>marriage and civil partnership</li>
    <li>pregnancy and maternity</li>
    <li>race</li>
    <li>religion or belief</li>
    <li>sex</li>
    <li>sexual orientation</li>
  </ul>

  <p>Some attributes can be used to accurately infer a protected characteristic. For example, someone’s age can be inferred by their date of birth. Other attributes may be used to deduce a protected characteristic with varying degrees of accuracy – for example, postcodes that indicate likely ethnicities.</p>

  <p>Proxies are not inherently harmful. For example, an organisation might use a proxy to monitor where a policy is having positive impact, or use that data to improve outcomes for people with protected characteristics where direct data does not exist.</p>

  <p>However, harmful outcomes can occur when a public body:</p>

  <ul>
    <li>is not aware that the data it’s processing can be proxies for protected characteristics</li>
    <li>does not consider the potential impact on people with protected characteristics</li>
    <li>does not measure or remedy impacts, as this can lead to unlawful discrimination and reduced equality of opportunity</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<h4 id="understand-impacted-groups">Understand impacted groups</h4>

<p>You should understand which individuals or groups could potentially benefit or be treated unfairly by your project, and which are most vulnerable to harm as a result.</p>

<p>These may be groups that share a <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/equality/equality-act-2010/protected-characteristics">protected characteristic</a>, or groups connected through different attributes such as their location, interests, the industry that they work in, and more.</p>

<p>Understanding and assessing the impact that a project may have on people, particularly in relation to the protected characteristics, helps public bodies demonstrate they comply with the <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr>.</p>

<p>You must assess the equality impact of your project:</p>

<ul>
  <li>before making any decisions to initiate a project, including procuring and development</li>
  <li>during implementation</li>
  <li>after implementation</li>
</ul>

<p>There’s no set way for you to record your equality considerations and your organisation may have its own Equality Impact Assessment (EIA) template for you to complete. We recommend that your EIA follows the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/how-consider-equality-policy-making-10-step-guide-public-bodies-england">10-step guide</a> published by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC). This will help you navigate what you must do to comply with the law, and what you should do to demonstrate best practice.</p>

<div class="call-to-action">
  <h4 id="representational-and-allocational-harms">Representational and allocational harms</h4>

  <p>Another way to understand fairness in your project is by considering the harms that it may cause. Harms are often categorised as either representational or allocational. Both concepts existed long before AI or data-enabled services, but technology means they may manifest in different ways and may need to be addressed differently.</p>

  <p>Representational harms concern how people are portrayed, including stereotyping, misrecognition and denigration. There are many cultural and institutional examples, such as in advertising, branding and entertainment. The impact of these harms can include reinforcing negative societal biases and social norms, psychological impacts and more.</p>

  <p>Representational harms are linked with the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed">third aim of the <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr></a> – ‘to foster good relations between people who have protected characteristics and those who do not’. Avoiding these harms will help you uphold your duty. </p>

  <p>Digital technologies, especially AI, are introducing new avenues for representational harms to occur. These harms are especially prevalent in generative AI models. The many different ways that AI may manifest in different types of content (text, video, image, audio) can make it particularly difficult to identify and mitigate.</p>

  <p>For example, large language models (LLMs) are known to encode biases and stereotypes from the text that they’re trained on. This may result in displaying gender bias when describing certain job roles, or reproduce negative stereotypes associated with protected demographic groups. Meanwhile, AI models that generate images have been found to typically generate images of light-skinned men when prompted to produce images of CEOs and judges, perpetuating harmful biases.</p>

  <p>Representational harms can also emerge in data sets. For instance, over-representation of minority groups in crime statistics could result in unfair and unlawful treatment.</p>

  <p>Allocational harms are linked with the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-psed">first and second aims of the <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr></a>, and concern how resources or opportunities are distributed among society. In particular, they impact operational departments responsible for providing access to any kind of service or resource. Examples include citizen-facing services that give access to medical procedures or medicines, or structural systems like the allocation of funding to build new schools. The impact of allocational harms can include loss of opportunity, reinforcing and perpetuating inequalities, and more.</p>

  <p>You should pay particular care to any algorithm employed where there are known historical inequalities, as the available training data is likely to encode these same biases. </p>

  <p>Though representational and allocational harms are described as distinct areas, they often overlap in the real world. For instance, a hiring system that is biased towards hiring women into nursing roles displays both representational and allocational harms. It stereotypes nursing as a job conducted by women, and increases the likelihood that the employment opportunity is allocated to a woman.</p>
</div>

<h4 id="understand-downstream-impacts">Understand downstream impacts</h4>

<p>The <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr> and any other fairness and equality requirements that you’ve identified for your work are ongoing. It’s important for you to regularly review the impacts that your work is having on people and society.</p>

<p>This can help you to determine whether:</p>

<ul>
  <li>you’re delivering the intended benefits you set out to deliver through your project, and that your investment is delivering value for taxpayers’ money</li>
  <li>your project is not leading to unintended consequences, including unlawful discrimination</li>
  <li>the actions you’ve taken to mitigate negative impact and maximise positive impact are having the intended effect</li>
</ul>

<p>Downstream impacts can be hard to predict. User research and journey mapping can help you understand the downstream impacts of your project. Civil society organisations may be able to provide important insights on potentially impacted groups. They may also be able to support the recruitment of user research participants in difficult-to-reach communities.</p>

<h4 id="building-for-fairness">Building for fairness</h4>

<p>If you determine that the risks and impacts identified in your EIA are acceptable, you’re likely to begin assembling a team to develop your project.</p>

<p>Having a diverse and multidisciplinary team can provide a strong foundation for building fairer tools and services. A diverse team is often able to spot issues early in the development process by bringing varied perspectives and lived experiences.</p>

<p>If it’s not possible to assemble a diverse team, you should note any potential gaps in understanding and proactively seek ways to engage with a variety of stakeholders. This might include through user testing, public engagement and, where possible, presenting ideas at internal or external community events.</p>

<p>You should note the potential blind spots and pay attention to these in testing and in conversation with civil society groups.</p>

<p>You should also apply these considerations when contracting out work to third-party organisations. For example, consider the diversity of their development teams and the methods they employ to mitigate potential gaps.</p>

<p>Fairness metrics are different ways to measure whether your data set is representative and free from bias, and whether AI systems treat people equitably. They can help to identify and quantify biases, and inform further development to ensure outcomes are not disproportionately favourable or harmful to certain demographic groups. </p>

<p>You should identify fairness metrics that are relevant to your project and address the potential harms you’ve identified. These can include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>demographic parity – where the proportion of positive or negative outcomes is the same for all groups</li>
  <li>equalised odds – a measurement of the accuracy of results (true-positive rate and false-positive rate) across different groups</li>
</ul>

<p>Fairness metrics are an evolving area. Each metric has relative strengths and weaknesses and research may uncover better methods. We recommend that you read current research on this topic to identify the most appropriate measurement for your project.</p>

<p>If you identify bias in your data or AI system, you must identify and implement mitigation techniques to reduce the risk and potential severity of harms. Apply these techniques anywhere in your project where bias occurs, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>data collection and processing methods</li>
  <li>bias in any systems, including AI systems</li>
  <li>biased impacts felt downstream</li>
</ul>

<p>Data on demographics, particularly related to protected characteristics, can support equality monitoring and meeting your obligations under the <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr>. You should consider privacy here, referring to the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/public-sector-equality-duty-and-data-protection">guidance on the use of personal data to support the <abbr title="Public Sector Equality Duty">PSED</abbr></a>.</p>

<h4 id="accessibility-and-fairness">Accessibility and fairness</h4>

<p>Fairness is not just about the outputs of your data set or AI system, but also about how people interact with the project and who can access and use it.</p>

<p>It’s important to remember that a proportion of the population does not have access to the internet or devices such as smartphones and tablets. Some groups are more at risk of being digitally excluded, including older people and people with disabilities. Some users may prefer non-digital channels.</p>

<p>This means that certain, often vulnerable, groups may not have access to digital services or be represented in data collected through digital platforms. As a result, their needs may be entirely missed or underrepresented.</p>

<p>You should actively conduct research with groups that may be excluded to understand their needs. You should also provide non-digital alternatives where possible, such as phone support or paper forms.</p>

<p>All public sector websites and applications must adhere to the <a rel="external" href="https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/">Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 requirements</a> unless they qualify for a specific <a rel="external" href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2018/952/pdfs/uksiem_20180952_en.pdf">exemption</a>. Even for exempt services, the WCAG 2.2 still provides useful guidance.</p>

<p>WCAG 2.2 provides information covering colour contrast, screen reader support, captions, and more. You should ensure that all content is written in plain language. Where appropriate, you should also make the content available in alternative languages and formats such as braille or British Sign Language. These and other similar changes may be considered <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/business/employing-people-workplace-adjustments/examples-reasonable-adjustments-practice">reasonable adjustments</a>. There are examples of reasonable adjustments applied to service delivery in the <a rel="external" href="https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/guidance/how-consider-equality-policy-making-10-step-guide-public-bodies-england">EHRC’s 10-step guide</a>. </p>

<h4 id="data-sets-and-labels">Data sets and labels</h4>

<p>Fairness may be negatively impacted by bias in data sets, or bias emerging from the way a data set is transformed and used. Here are some of the ways in which your data sets may be biased.</p>

<h4 id="representation-bias">Representation bias</h4>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p>Data may be biased if it’s not representative – for example, not including enough examples from a particular group, or not including the group at all. This could cause higher levels of inaccuracy for impacted groups, leading to inaccurate decision making. It could also cause lower levels of performance, which may result in frustrating user experiences or barriers to accessing a service.<br><br>Minority groups are inherently more likely to be underrepresented, which may lead to compounding negative effects. In these instances, oversampling (capturing more information about the concerned group) may be beneficial.<br><br>Certain locations have historically been better researched than others. On a global scale, the Global North (North America and Europe) tends to be more represented in data sets when compared to the Global South (Africa, South Asia and Latin America). Within countries, major cities tend to be more highly represented when compared to rural areas and informal settlements.</p>
</div>

<h4 id="societal-bias">Societal bias</h4>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p>Bias may still be present in a data set even if it’s fully representative of the population, due to biases present in our current and past society. Societal bias occurs when the data we collect, generate and use reflects discriminatory patterns present in society.</p>
</div>

<h4 id="data-aggregation-bias">Data aggregation bias</h4>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p>This occurs when data is grouped or aggregated in a way that distorts the results of the analysis. For example, over-aggregating ethnic groups in demographic data – such as by only using ‘White’, ‘Black’, ‘Asian’ or ‘Other’ – can mask differences between groups, such as ‘Gypsy, Roma and Traveller (GRT) communities’.<br><br>The act of grouping data can obscure important variations and nuances present within the subgroups or individual data points, leading to a misrepresentation of the underlying relationships. Note that <a rel="external" href="https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/fairness/?modulepage=design-biases">aggregation bias in AI</a> has a different meaning, referring to instances where trained models are applied in a one-size-fits-all manner. </p>
</div>

<h4 id="measurement-bias">Measurement bias</h4>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p>This arises from discrepancies between gathered data and real-world experiences or events. This can happen due to flawed measurement processes and inconsistent or inaccurate data labelling. Measurement bias may also <a rel="external" href="https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/fairness/?modulepage=design-biases">be present in AI systems</a>.<br><br>Data labelling practices (the process of assigning a tag, name or description to data to provide additional context) can also be a source of bias. Labels may be assigned inaccurately, and improperly designed labelling schemes may make it impossible to be accurate in all cases.</p>
</div>

<h4 id="ongoing-fairness-commitments">Ongoing fairness commitments</h4>

<p>Your fairness commitments do not end once the project has gone live. Unforeseen problems may emerge in the real world. Shifts in the societal, cultural, economic and technological landscapes may mean that your project does not remain fair throughout its life cycle.</p>

<p>It’s vital that you continue to monitor the performance of your project post-implementation, including fairness and inclusion. You should include fairness and equality clauses in contractual arrangements with any third-party suppliers. Your monitoring should include information from suppliers if aspects of your project are procured or contracted out to third-party organisations. The Local Government Association has guidance on <a rel="external" href="https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning">responsibly buying AI</a>.</p>

<p>You should maintain user feedback and issue reporting systems throughout the system’s life, and make these visible to users. Consider what resources you should make available throughout the life cycle of the system, to fix newly identified fairness problems and to remediate harms. You should disaggregate your investigations into this feedback to understand the impact on different groups.</p>

<h4 id="disaggregated-feedback">Disaggregated feedback</h4>

<p>Aggregated feedback – the combined feedback from all the groups on your project – may help explain technical aspects of the project’s performance. However, it’s unlikely to tell the full story. </p>

<p>For instance, your project may involve a chatbot which receives 95% positive feedback from users. While this statistic may seem positive on the surface, it’s critical to understand which groups of people are satisfied, and which fall into the 5% that are dissatisfied. This may reveal that the dissatisfied group aligns with a particular protected characteristic. Identifying this provides an opportunity to mitigate impacts and build a fairer and more inclusive service.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub">Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (<abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>)</a> provides a way to publish information about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>fairness metrics – for example, those included in your EIA</li>
  <li>activities such as testing and bias mitigations</li>
</ul>

<p>If your project involves an algorithmic tool that’s in scope of the standard, your transparency record could provide a strong platform to communicate the fairness attributes of your project.</p>

<h3 id="recommended-actions-2">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>define fairness – understanding what fairness and associated risks and opportunities mean in your project, and how you might measure that across its life cycle</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>understand your users – identify the groups most likely to be positively or negatively impacted by your project, and how this relates to the protected characteristics described in the Equality Act 2010</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>consider which proxies might relate to the protected characteristics in your data set and be mindful and transparent about their use and purpose</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>complete an EIA and consider publishing it alongside your <abbr title="Data Protection Impact Assessment">DPIA</abbr> and <abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr> record (if relevant) for transparency and accountability</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>include diverse views – consider the diversity of your project team and any third parties you’re contracting</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>collect feedback and data throughout your project to ensure that it continues to be fair and delivers its intended benefits, as society and user groups change</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>regularly update your EIA</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="privacy-section">Privacy</h2>

<p>Privacy is a complex ethical, legal, technological and social principle. It protects individual autonomy, meaning people should have the freedom to live, think, choose, socialise and more without undue observation or interference. </p>

<p>In a digital and data-driven society, personal data is routinely collected, processed and used by public sector bodies to generate insights, develop AI tools and make decisions. This impacts peoples’ privacy and needs to be protected in line with ethical and legal obligations. </p>

<p>A failure to respect individuals’ privacy can lead to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>loss of public trust</li>
  <li>harm to people, particularly vulnerable individuals</li>
  <li>regulatory risk</li>
</ul>

<p>Privacy is not just a legal compliance exercise, but a fundamental human right that fosters trust and empowers individuals in the digital age. This guidance explores ethical responsibilities that extend beyond legal compliance, but you must still comply with the law at all times by following:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-and-the-eu/data-protection-and-the-eu-in-detail/the-uk-gdpr/">UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK <abbr title="General Data Protection Regulation">GDPR</abbr></a>)</li>
  <li>the <a rel="external" href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2018/12/contents/enacted">Data Protection Act 2018</a>
</li>
  <li>the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/data-use-and-access-act-2025">Data (Use and Access) Act 2025</a>
</li>
  <li>any other applicable privacy legislation</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="what-privacy-means-in-practice">What privacy means in practice</h3>

<p>You must design and build privacy into your project from the start. This includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the very first decisions you make about what information you intend to record</li>
  <li>every way that the data, or AI system built using this data, is used throughout your project</li>
  <li>the safe decommissioning of the system and data set</li>
</ul>

<p>This concept is referred to in the UK <abbr title="General Data Protection Regulation">GDPR</abbr> as <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/guide-to-accountability-and-governance/data-protection-by-design-and-default/">privacy by design and default</a>.</p>

<p>Privacy is about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>autonomy – citizens’ capacity to live their own lives and make decisions based on their own motives and reasons, free from external manipulation (provided actions are within the law)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>confidentiality – data can be both sensitive and private, and confidentiality is the duty to ensure it’s only shared in appropriate and authorised ways</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>dignity – this is about the intrinsic value of all people, not as data points, but as people; it means ensuring that any methods of data collection, processing and use of AI do not exploit, humiliate or dehumanise people</p>

<h4 id="purpose-and-benefit-in-the-context-of-data-protection">Purpose and benefit in the context of data protection</h4>

<p>Before you start collecting, sharing or using data, you should clearly understand:</p>

<ul>
  <li>why you’re processing the data (the purpose)</li>
  <li>what public benefit this will bring</li>
</ul>

<p>The scope of your project should be strictly limited to your identified purpose throughout its life cycle. You should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>engage with your organisation’s data protection officer (DPO)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>consider whether your purpose could be easily understood by someone with no technical background in the domain – people must be able to understand your project so they can provide clear, informed and unambiguous consent</p>
  </li>
  <li>clearly record the purpose and benefit of your project – for example, who benefits, and how you’ll know if you achieve your aims
    <ul>
      <li>examples of measures could include cost savings, reduced waiting times or the number of people who receive support</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>explain why AI is the right tool for this purpose, if your project uses AI</li>
</ul>

<p>Articulating and recording your purpose and public benefit at this stage can help to avoid scope creep and may help you comply with regulation such as the UK <abbr title="General Data Protection Regulation">GDPR</abbr>.</p>

<h3 id="scoping-and-data-acquisition">Scoping and data acquisition</h3>

<p>If your project involves the collection or use of any personal data, you should start by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>establishing precisely what information you need to meet your purpose</li>
  <li>creating a high-level map of your data flow before this begins – for example, a document that lists each data element as a line item, and records why it’s necessary, proportionate and what the effect would be if it was not used</li>
</ul>

<p>The data you request and acquire must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which it is processed. This is known as data minimisation. The Information Commissioner’s Office has guidance on <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/">data minimisation</a>, including how to determine if the use of data is adequate, relevant and limited.</p>

<p>Consider whether you could use anonymised or <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-insights/ai-insights-synthetic-data-html">synthetic data</a> to replace some or all of the personal data your project requires. If personally identifiable information is essential for your project, ensure that the risks are proportional to the benefits.</p>

<p>Your project might not itself gather or process personal data. For example, if you procure an AI model from a third party or use a pre-trained model. Here you must still ensure that any personal data used to train these models meets your privacy standards and complies with relevant legislation. The UK Statistics Authority (UKSA) provides an <a rel="external" href="https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/ethical-considerations-relating-to-the-creation-and-use-of-synthetic-data/pages/6/">Ethics Checklist</a> relating to the creation and use of synthetic data which may support these decisions.</p>

<p>The Local Government Association has guidance on <a rel="external" href="https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/responsible-buying-how-build-equality-data-protection-your-ai-commissioning">responsibly buying AI</a> which discusses data protection.</p>

<h3 id="privacy-by-design-and-default">Privacy by design and default</h3>

<p>There are 2 main principles to guide the development of your system or service:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>privacy by design – making design and development decisions from the very start that enhance privacy objectives</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>privacy by default - ensuring that default settings for the product or service are the most privacy-preserving options</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/privacy-enhancing-technologies-cost-benefit-awareness-tool/cost-benefit-awareness-tool">Privacy enhancing technologies (PETs)</a> can help to achieve a privacy-by-design approach.</p>

<p>Transparency can also support privacy. Design methods and notices to explain:</p>

<ul>
  <li>what data you collect</li>
  <li>why you need the data</li>
  <li>how the data is used</li>
  <li>how long the data will be stored for</li>
</ul>

<p>A good principle to uphold is that nobody should be surprised about how their data is being used.</p>

<p>AI systems require greater attention and introduce new risks. For example, AI systems may re-identify individuals that were believed to be anonymised by linking information with other data sets, or information made available when it was trained. In addition, large language model (LLM) tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot may ‘memorise’ sensitive or personal information contained within their training data sets and leak this private information during their operation.</p>

<p>To mitigate this risk we recommend that you: </p>

<ul>
  <li>treat all models that have been trained on data about people as though they potentially contain personally identifiable data, and make security and risk-based decisions accordingly</li>
  <li>where appropriate, manage access via an <a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/application-programming-interfaces-apis">Application Programming Interface (API)</a> to limit information leakage, and apply PETs such as Trusted Research Environments to protect data sets</li>
  <li>integrate re-identification risk into your security and risk management processes</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="test-and-validate">Test and validate </h3>

<p>Before going live with a new service, you must thoroughly test to ensure that it works as intended and does not introduce new privacy risks. </p>

<p>You should conduct testing throughout the build phases, and repeat it after your service goes live. This is particularly important if any changes are made to the system, data source(s), or when there are significant societal changes that may impact the service.</p>

<p>Where possible, you should conduct tests with anonymised or synthetic data. If it’s necessary to test with personal data, make sure you do this in a secure environment with strict limitations on access.</p>

<p>Red teaming exercises may help to probe the service or AI system. Pay particular attention to any:</p>

<ul>
  <li>data that may be exposed which links the protected characteristics as defined in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/equality-act-2010-guidance">Equality Act 2010</a>
</li>
  <li>health and location data</li>
  <li>data that may relate to vulnerabilities</li>
</ul>

<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/">National Cyber Security Centre</a> has guidance on protecting personal data, including the <a rel="external" href="https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/cyber-assessment-framework">Cyber Assessment Framework</a>.</p>

<h3 id="be-transparent-and-give-users-control">Be transparent and give users control</h3>

<p>Users who are impacted by your service should be able to understand what information you collect, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>what it will be used for</li>
  <li>how long you’ll retain it</li>
  <li>how they can manage their privacy settings</li>
</ul>

<p>This information should be clearly available at the point of use. Use clear and accessible language in privacy documentation, avoiding jargon and legalistic terms where possible. When interacting with the public, we recommend offering configurable privacy options. A good rule of thumb is to make it as easy to opt-in as it is to opt-out, give people free choices and respect users’ autonomy. You can also review previous <a rel="external" href="https://www.bi.team/publications/active-online-choices-designing-to-empower-users-2/">government research</a> into how different ways of collecting consent can impact users’ behaviour and enable ‘active’ online choices.</p>

<p>There are basic requirements for consent to be legally valid. It must be properly informed, freely given, specific and unambiguous. If you rely on the consent of data subjects, you also need to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>provide an effective and straightforward way for them to withdraw their consent</li>
  <li>tell users what withdrawal means for the service they receive</li>
</ul>

<p>The concept of ‘freely given consent’ implies providing a real choice for the data subject. Any element of inappropriate pressure or influence which could affect the outcome of that choice renders the consent invalid. The law takes a certain imbalance between the controller and the data subject into consideration.</p>

<p>For example, in an employer-employee relationship the employee may worry that refusal to consent may have negative consequences for their employment relationship. Similar issues of imbalance arise between people and the state, where there is little or no choice for people when it comes to many public services. For example, there’s no alternative when it comes to seeking welfare benefits, or applying for a passport. Here, consent can only be a valid lawful basis for processing in a few exceptional circumstances.</p>

<p>We also encourage a privacy-by-default approach, where the most privacy-preserving settings are enabled by default unless the user decides to choose otherwise.</p>

<p>Transparency extends beyond privacy notices. You should design processes to ensure users understand how their data is being used at every point. This builds trust and supports informed consent. </p>

<p>You should review your service at important points, including milestones and significant updates. This will ensure that you’re still achieving your intended goals and aligning users with your use of data. Even if your service does not change, societal expectations may.</p>

<h3 id="plan-for-and-respond-to-data-breaches">Plan for and respond to data breaches</h3>

<p>Even with strong safeguards, it’s impossible to guarantee that breaches will never happen. Prepare in advance to ensure you have answers to the following questions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>who investigates suspected breaches and how?</li>
  <li>how can you contain potential breaches and secure data?</li>
  <li>how will you inform impacted users of a breach?</li>
  <li>what support will you offer to anyone harmed by a breach?</li>
</ul>

<p>A well-handled breach can reduce or eliminate harm and preserve public trust, while a poorly handled one may cause lasting damage.</p>

<p>Ensure that your safeguards and processes evolve and adapt to a changing threat landscape. </p>

<h3 id="decommissioning">Decommissioning</h3>

<p>You must retire all platforms at an appropriate time.</p>

<p>This may be when:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the service is no longer needed</li>
  <li>your purpose is better met, or greater public benefit is achieved, with a new service</li>
  <li>the public benefit of the current system is no longer meeting social expectations</li>
</ul>

<p>When decommissioning a service, make sure you honour data retention limits, including any data which has been stored or processed by third-party organisations. </p>

<p>Where there’s a legal duty or other obligation to retain certain data, ensure this is done securely and with strict access controls, and that confidentiality is protected.</p>

<p>We encourage teams to record, and publish in their internal knowledge bases, any lessons learned about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>how privacy risks were managed</li>
  <li>public attitudes towards data sharing and AI – ensuring that these findings are aligned with any agreements that were in place with research participants</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="recommended-actions-3">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>involve information governance teams early in the project design process – this will help you to comply with privacy and data protection legislation, and plan resources effectively so that support is available for project teams when needed</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>record the purpose and benefit to understand why any data collection is necessary and whether it’s balanced against privacy risks, and use this record to ensure your project does not grow beyond its defined scope</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>embed privacy by design and default from the outset – undertake a Data Protection Impact Assessment (<abbr title="Data Protection Impact Assessment">DPIA</abbr>) to access and mitigate against data privacy risks</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>adopt data minimisation techniques – ensure that the data you collect and process is the lowest amount required to achieve your purpose</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>facilitate data subjects’ rights – build in mechanisms for data access and correction, and ensure consent is informed and meaningful</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use PETs where possible, applying techniques such as anonymisation or the use of synthetic data</p>
  </li>
  <li>share data responsibly by having a robust, privacy-preserving governance regime that safeguards:
    <ul>
      <li>security</li>
      <li>lawful basis</li>
      <li>explicit retention or deletion protocols,</li>
      <li>provisions that secure individuals’ privacy and data protection rights as part of sharing agreements and records</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>consider the impact of AI – explore additional privacy risks that AI systems may introduce, such as re-identification of individuals in data sets
    <ul>
      <li>using public AI tools, such as ChatGPT, can increase the risk of data leakage</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>be transparent by providing clear privacy notices that tell users exactly how their data is being used and their options, and give users a free choice to configure settings</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>prepare for breaches – develop clear plans and assign responsibilities to investigate and tackle any suspected data breaches</p>
  </li>
  <li>plan for decommissioning – create plans for data archival or deletion at an appropriate time, considering how long the data will be needed for the service you’re providing and the life cycle of your project</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="environmental-sustainability-section">Environmental sustainability</h2>

<p>Environmental sustainability means thinking about the wider impact of your project on people and the planet, and being mindful about the resources you use every day. It’s important to consider this from the start, as it can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure.</p>

<p>For data and AI projects, acting sustainably means:</p>

<ul>
  <li>using only the necessary resources</li>
  <li>protecting natural resources and using them responsibly</li>
  <li>designing systems that last and are easy to maintain</li>
</ul>

<p>Sustainability also includes social responsibility. This means supporting inclusion, fairness and human rights in how technologies are designed, manufactured, used and disposed of.</p>

<h3 id="what-environmental-sustainability-means-in-practice">What environmental sustainability means in practice</h3>

<p>Data and AI can support environmental goals, such as predicting weather patterns or monitoring biodiversity levels. However, developing and training AI models, especially large language models (LLMs), requires the use of critical minerals, energy, water and computing resources.</p>

<p>This means that you should consider environmental impact:</p>

<ul>
  <li>at every level in your organisation – from analysts to senior decision-makers</li>
  <li>across the entire life cycle of your tool or project – including when it is decommissioned or handed over to another team</li>
</ul>

<p>The complex supply chains of data-driven technologies, and the natural resources required to build them, mean they can have a long-lasting impact on people and the planet. For example, the mining of raw materials to build computing chips and other AI infrastructure. This has a significant environmental cost and impact on the health and wellbeing of workers and affected communities.</p>

<p>Setting clear sustainability objectives and using greener software practices will help make sustainability a core part of your project design.</p>

<p>You should also consider whether there’s a reasonable trade-off between the benefits of your tool or system and its environmental impact. There may be trade-offs between different ethical principles. For example, the use of a more energy-intensive algorithm that’s also more explainable, or that brings wider benefits and value to the public. Make sure you clearly document when you’ve made decisions about trade-offs, and the governance processes you used.</p>

<h3 id="measuring-monitoring-and-evaluating-environmental-impact">Measuring, monitoring and evaluating environmental impact</h3>

<p>Sustainability reporting for cloud and wider digital services is an evolving area where research and development is ongoing. This means it may be challenging to identify appropriate metrics, and the reliability of reporting may differ across suppliers. The following tools and methods will provide you with a starting point.</p>

<p>Before you begin building a tool or system, think about:</p>

<ul>
  <li>whether AI is the best technology or tool for the task – there may be alternatives that provide as good, or better, results and require less resource-intensive training and development</li>
  <li>project size and complexity – how much data will be processed, the number of end users, bandwidth and latency requirements, prompt efficiency</li>
  <li>software requirements – including model type </li>
  <li>hardware requirements – such as data centre usage or Internet of Things (IoT) devices</li>
</ul>

<p>There are various environmental factors that you should monitor and manage across the life cycle of your project.</p>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p><strong>Electricity consumption</strong><br>Data centres use large amounts of electricity for running servers and data processing. Some even use fossil fuel-based generators due to a lack of capacity in local grids. Using electricity results in the release of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane and nitrous oxide, which contribute to climate change.</p>
</div>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p><strong>Water consumption</strong><br>For example, data centres require significant amounts of fresh water for cooling systems and to avoid hardware failure.</p>
</div>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p><strong>Consumption of raw materials</strong><br>The mining of raw materials, for example to build computing chips and other AI infrastructure, has a significant environmental cost and impact on the health and wellbeing of workers and affected communities.</p>
</div>

<div role="note" aria-label="Information" class="application-notice info-notice">
  <p><strong>E-waste</strong><br>Electronic waste (e-waste) from discarded electrical devices contains rare earth materials such as neodymium; if not disposed of properly, these materials can contaminate soil and water, and release noxious gases into the atmosphere, posing extremely harmful risks to biodiversity, human health and the environment.</p>
</div>

<p>In your project, consider how the following may impact resource consumption:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>data set size – large data sets require more energy to store and process, especially when used to train AI systems, and you should also consider the impact of the resolution or bit rate of the data sets</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>data type – generating or handling high-volume text (for example, training LLMs), video or image data is typically more energy-intensive than other data types because it requires more intensive computing, memory and bandwidth workloads</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>data velocity – high-velocity data (such as real-time streaming) increases compute load</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>architecture – using technologies like virtualisation can reduce energy consumption, hardware needs and associated resource demands by allowing data to be accessed and queried without the need for transfer or duplication; adopting modular design can help promote reuse and reduce future resource consumption</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>storage – data storage has an ongoing carbon footprint, primarily in data centres, due to the continuous generation of heat and use of water and electricity to run them; establishing and running data centres also involves biodiversity loss from land clearing, droughts caused by fresh water extraction, e-waste and pollutants</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>model type – multi-purpose, generative architectures typically use more resources than task-specific systems; you should always explore different options, including not using AI at all, before choosing a technical approach</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>model size – LLMs and other generative AI systems generally require more energy and emit more carbon compared to running a single prediction on a trained model</p>
  </li>
  <li>location – try to run algorithms in locations with higher uses of renewable energy to reduce your carbon footprint
    <ul>
      <li>you can use electricity maps to understand the electricity usage and emissions of different regions</li>
      <li>you should adhere to any relevant data residency rules if selecting a server location based on energy mix</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>time of day – the source of energy on the grid changes during the day; where it’s viable, you can make carrying out computationally complex processing tasks more environmentally friendly by shifting the time they take place, even by a few hours, to when energy generation is cleaner</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="selecting-metrics">Selecting metrics</h4>

<p>You should select appropriate metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs) that can be tracked over time. There are several ways of quantifying environmental impact across the development and deployment phases of a project.</p>

<p>Common metrics include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>carbon footprint (CO2-equivalent emissions)</li>
  <li>energy consumption (measured kilowatt-hour or kWh)</li>
  <li>compute efficiency (for example, FLOPs per watt – how many calculations a system can perform for every watt of power it uses)</li>
  <li>water consumption (measured in litres)</li>
</ul>

<p>There are some open-source tools that can help to analyse and measure the environmental impact of a data or AI project:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://digitaldecarb.org/data-carbon-ladder/">Data Carbon Ladder</a> can provide an estimated data CO2 footprint for your project, highlighting areas to improve to minimise environmental impact – this tool is particularly useful at the project planning stage</li>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://codecarbon.io/">CodeCarbon</a> is a software package that integrates into your Python codebase; it estimates the amount of CO2 produced by the cloud or personal computing resources used to execute the code</li>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://mlco2.github.io/impact/">ML CO2 Impact</a> is a free machine learning emissions calculator which provides information about the raw carbon emissions produced and the approximate offset carbon emissions of a given project</li>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/26686">Carburacy</a> is a carbon-aware accuracy measure for evaluating the eco-sustainability of Natural Language Processing (NLP) models</li>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://ecologits.ai/latest/">EcoLogits</a> is a tool that can help to track the energy consumption and environmental impacts of using generative AI models through APIs</li>
</ul>

<p>It’s important to note that there are often trade-offs when selecting particular metrics over others, and some impacts will be harder to quantify. For example, carbon emissions may be more easily tracked but neglect a tool’s broader impact, like water usage or impact on local communities.</p>

<h4 id="minimising-environmental-impact">Minimising environmental impact</h4>

<p>There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to minimising your environmental impact, but even small actions can make a big difference. Depending on your project, there are many ways to make a positive change.</p>

<p>If you’re handling or analysing data, you should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>minimise the data you’re collecting and using – collect only the data necessary to meet the research or project objectives</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use data compression and aggregation to reduce storage and bandwidth requirements – for example, compressing data before transmission (using formats like GZIP or Parquet) can help to save bandwidth</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>regularly review whether the data you hold to help reduce its volume – consider whether there’s any redundant, obsolete or trivial (ROT) data that can be safely deleted</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>avoid re-running entire pipelines – use incremental workflows which only re-process new or changed data</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use cloud storage tiers, scaling and right-sizing instances – this can help to optimise data storage allocation by, for example, automatically moving infrequently accessed (‘cold’) data to lower-energy storage</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use narrow prompts for generative AI tools – shorter or more focused prompts typically result in less processing time and improved accuracy of responses</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use techniques such as virtualisation to reduce duplication</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>design modular components for potential reuse in future projects</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>If you’re building AI or algorithmic tools (including using pre-trained models), you should:<br>
- consider reuse – where you can meet the requirements of your project lawfully and safely, consider reusing existing models or services (for example, open source, or models trained for previous projects) over building and retraining from scratch</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>explore how you might be able to achieve comparable results using a smaller data set – for model training, evaluate whether a curated subset can achieve similar performance compared to using a full data set</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use smaller models for specific tasks – this can help to reduce cost and power consumption, making the technology easier to deploy</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use model optimisation techniques to improve performance, efficiency and accuracy – this might include quantisation (converting input values to smaller output values to reduce compute and memory requirements) or model pruning to remove unused or unnecessary parameters</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>clean up unused resources, such as idle or outdated coding notebooks</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>introduce early stopping rules to stop training when a model’s performance plateaus – this can prevent redundant training cycles</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>find out about the environmental credentials of models – if you’re using open-source models, you can find information on environmental impact on the <a rel="external" href="https://huggingface.co/open-llm-leaderboard">Hugging Face open LLM Leaderboard</a> or <a rel="external" href="https://ecologits.ai/latest/">EcoLogits</a> </p>
    <ul>
      <li>if you cannot find information about a particular model, consider whether you could achieve similar results with a more transparent alternative</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>If you’re using a third party supplier, you should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>include sustainability as a criteria during the supplier selection process – ask about the energy consumption and carbon footprint of the AI models and infrastructure before engaging a service</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>find information about the broader ethical practices of the organisation, such as labour standards and sustainability commitments – be aware of potential greenwashing terms and practices</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ask suppliers what happens to hardware at the end of life – for example, if hardware is refurbished, donated or responsibly recycled</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual">Service Manual</a> also has guidance on how to build more <a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/environmentally-sustainable-services">environmentally sustainable digital services</a> in government.</p>

<h3 id="recommended-actions-4">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>explore and evaluate alternative solutions – the latest technology or innovation isn’t always best for the job, so explore different options, including simple and low-energy options, before selecting an approach</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>consider reuse of existing models – advocate for the use of open-source models where source code, data and model weights are available for community reuse, rather than using energy to retrain or build similar models</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>select suitable metrics for measuring and assessing environmental impact – this can be a complex task but is vital for ensuring proper stewardship of data and AI projects</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>evaluate the sustainability credentials and practices of third-party providers, including their use of renewable energy</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>raise awareness about the environmental and social impact of digital technologies – share knowledge with colleagues and look for opportunities to bring sustainability into training and discussions</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="societal-impact-section">Societal impact</h2>

<p>The use of data and AI is already changing how people live and work. For example, the accessibility of tools such as ChatGPT has started to reshape how we undertake daily tasks. These rapid changes raise important questions about how digital technologies are used, and how they affect society.</p>

<p>Societal impact refers to the effects that data and AI can have on individuals, communities, social structures and economies. This includes both positive and negative impacts.</p>

<p>For example, adopting chatbots in public sector call centres might reduce costs, boost productivity and allow for faster handling of cases. However, it can also lead to job losses, or create a less personal relationship between government and the public that leaves citizens feeling disempowered.</p>

<p>Taking care to respect other principles such as privacy and fairness can have wider societal impacts, building trust and improving education and health outcomes.</p>

<p>Even relatively simple technical solutions can have significant societal impact. For example, an automated form that checks eligibility for a service might unintentionally exclude people if it does not account for different living situations or types of identification. This could stop people from getting the support they need and reduce trust in public services.</p>

<h3 id="what-societal-impact-means-in-practice">What societal impact means in practice</h3>

<p>To understand how data and AI can impact society, you need to understand the broader social and technical context in which they are used and built.</p>

<p>For example, the context and mechanisms of data collection can have a significant impact on who is, and is not, represented in a data set. As a result, an entire group of people might be excluded or underrepresented. In the context of government, this could lead to poor or even discriminatory policy decisions.</p>

<p>Both complex supply chains and resource usage of data and AI have a significant societal impact. This includes the displacement of local communities, and food and water scarcity in already vulnerable parts of the world. You must consider what knock-on effects your project might have on communities.</p>

<p>Proactive public and stakeholder engagement is critical to understand the potential societal impact of a tool or system. Engaging with stakeholders can help to build trust and improve adoption of AI tools and systems.</p>

<p>You should consider:</p>

<ul>
  <li>how data was collected and processed</li>
  <li>who technology affects and how</li>
  <li>how and where data or a particular technology is used</li>
  <li>how a data-driven system is designed and built</li>
</ul>

<p>Data and AI tools can help improve public services and benefit society. However, they also raise societal risks that must be managed, such as:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>unfair treatment – the use of data or AI systems can lead to unequal outcomes, such as people being treated differently based on race, gender or other protected characteristics</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>misinformation and disinformation – AI tools can be used to create misleading or deliberately false content, including text and images, which is then circulated online at scale; this can contribute to the spread of hate speech, in some cases causing widespread distrust and political violence</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>changes to jobs – automation may reduce demand for some roles and increase the need for new skills; the increased adoption of AI tools has the potential to reshape the world of work, including work becoming less fulfilling</p>
  </li>
  <li>
