    <p>changes to relationships – using technology can change the way people relate to each other, removing opportunities for care, connection and community that can combat loneliness and build trust and community cohesion</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ownership of creative work – the use of generative AI, typically trained on web-scraped data, such as original images and academic articles, raises legal questions about intellectual property and the ownership of content</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>power imbalances – the information about many AI tools is not transparent or accessible; this can give more control to those who build or use them, and less to those affected, leading to distrust, disaffection and disempowerment</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>adverse impacts on human rights and fundamental freedoms – irresponsibly designed or misused AI technologies can, among other things:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>harm human dignity</li>
      <li>damage physical, psychological and moral integrity</li>
      <li>undermine freedoms of expression and assembly</li>
      <li>infringe on the right to private and family life</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<h4 id="understanding-stakeholders">Understanding stakeholders</h4>

<p>To understand your project’s societal impact, identify who could be affected and how. The act of public engagement can help to build trust and improve adoption of new tools and services.</p>

<p>At the start of your project, you should make sure that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>your project has a clear purpose</li>
  <li>there’s a clear public benefit</li>
  <li>you’re designing with humans in mind and in a human-centred way</li>
</ul>

<p>Ethical use of data and AI means listening to different perspectives and checking that your tools work as intended. Otherwise, you could unintentionally exclude people or cause harm.</p>

<p>You should ask:</p>

<ul>
  <li>who could be negatively or positively affected? </li>
  <li>do the risks outweigh the expected benefits?</li>
  <li>how are the risks and benefits distributed across different groups? </li>
  <li>what might be the long-term consequences?</li>
</ul>

<p>To better understand the lived experiences of users, it can be helpful to use qualitative and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/ethnographic-study-qualitative-studies">ethnographic methods</a> such as observations, informal conversations or interviews. Think about how different people experience services, including colleagues who will be using the tools.</p>

<p>Consider:</p>

<ul>
  <li>age</li>
  <li>disability</li>
  <li>gender reassignment</li>
  <li>marriage and civil partnership</li>
  <li>pregnancy and maternity</li>
  <li>race</li>
  <li>religion or belief</li>
  <li>sex and sexual orientation</li>
  <li>income</li>
  <li>access to technology</li>
  <li>other attributes relevant to your project</li>
</ul>

<p>To better understand the views of, or potential impacts on, wider stakeholders and the public, consider proactive stakeholder or public engagement. For a helpful overview, refer to the <a rel="external" href="https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/sustainability-1/?modulepage=stakeholder-engagement">Alan Turing Institute’s stakeholder engagement overview</a> or <a rel="external" href="https://connectedbydata.org/topics/participation">resources from Connected by Data</a>.</p>

<p>You should factor in ways to empower the public and workers who may be using data and AI tools. To adopt AI safely and effectively, teams should have:</p>

<ul>
  <li>suitable training and resources</li>
  <li>a working environment that considers and prioritises broader ‘human’ factors – including cultural shifts, organisational change and skill development</li>
</ul>

<p>To learn more, refer to the guidance on <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-human-centred-approach-to-scaling-and-de-risking-ai-tools/the-people-factor-a-human-centred-approach-to-scaling-ai-tools-html">a human-centred approach to scaling AI tools</a>.</p>

<p>You should continually revisit user needs throughout your project. The Service Manual explains more about <a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/start-by-learning-user-needs">user needs</a>.</p>

<h4 id="identifying-harms-and-benefits">Identifying harms and benefits</h4>

<p>A practical way to identify the harms and benefits of a data or AI project is to bring teams and affected people and communities together to discuss:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the intended and unintended consequences of the system</li>
  <li>what could go wrong</li>
  <li>what can be done to mitigate risks</li>
</ul>

<p>Not all harms and potential impacts are obvious. You should factor in time during the project planning stage to run workshops, following practices such as The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-model-for-responsible-innovation/the-model-for-responsible-innovation">Model for Responsible Innovation</a> or <a rel="external" href="https://doteveryone.org.uk/project/consequence-scanning/">Consequence Scanning</a>. The Model for Responsible Innovation is a practical tool created by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) to help teams across the public sector to innovate responsibly with data and AI. You can use the model to run red teaming workshops with teams developing data-driven technology.</p>

<p>Horizon or risk scanning workshops can help to create an open dialogue, so team members, colleagues and external stakeholders can raise concerns and ideas. As part of this scanning, include structured reflection on the team’s perspectival limitations and stakeholder diversity to mitigate blind spots. Often, project teams do not sufficiently reflect the social and demographic characteristics of affected groups. This can limit inclusion of impacted viewpoints and reduce the ability to identify, understand and weigh risks, benefits and trade‑offs.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-guide-to-inclusive-social-research-practices/a-guide-to-inclusive-social-research-practices">Positionality‑aware</a> analysis, coupled with meaningful engagement, can surface concerns and opportunities more effectively and equitably. Adopting this reflective and inclusive approach can help to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>identify risks before they happen</li>
  <li>make more informed decisions about design and use</li>
  <li>align projects more closely with organisational and societal values</li>
  <li>build systems that are safer, more trustworthy and more contextually responsive to user needs and interests</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="continuous-monitoring-and-evaluation">Continuous monitoring and evaluation</h4>

<p>Usually, the full effect of a project or tool is not fully known during design and development. This means teams may miss risks or unintended consequences until the system is used in the real world.</p>

<p>You should continuously monitor for potentially harmful societal impacts, and actively address them. This includes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>providing ways for users and other stakeholders to give feedback – such as adding a feedback form to a service or webpage, or running follow-up user research sessions</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>making adjustments based on user engagement and testing – such as adapting your design or approach when you identify risks</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>being transparent about decisions – keep a clear record of what was changed, why, and who was involved; refer to the <a href="#transparency-section">Transparency</a> section for more on this</p>
  </li>
  <li>monitoring the system post-deployment for any unintended impacts of the system, such as factors relating to workforce engagement or public trust
    <ul>
      <li>evaluate outcomes based on demographic segments, for example by checking if the tool is affecting groups in unequal ways</li>
      <li>think about how the introduction of a data-driven tool or approach could inadvertently embed a particular worldview</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>reviewing and evaluating on a continuous basis, and when real-world conditions change – pay attention to the dynamic and changing character of the technology (for example, AI models are regularly updated) and to the shifting conditions of the real-world environments in which systems will be embedded</p>
  </li>
  <li>considering independent evaluation – commissioning external evaluation, such as audits, can provide impartial perspectives that can help with building trust</li>
</ul>

<p>For more guidance, refer to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the <a rel="external" href="https://testing-ai-standards.github.io/cross-gov-ai-testing-framework/">AI Testing and Assurance Framework for Public Sector</a> – this covers continuous monitoring and improvement of AI systems post-deployment</li>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/guidance-on-the-impact-evaluation-of-ai-interventions-html">Guidance on the Impact Evaluation of AI Interventions</a> for best practice in carrying out a robust impact evaluation of programmes and initiatives using AI systems in central government or the delivery of public services</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="recommended-actions-5">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>write down project objectives in non-technical terms, so that you understand the objectives before jumping to a technical solution
    <ul>
      <li>for example, ‘the project seeks to [enhance public safety, reduce waiting times, improve customer experience]’</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>involve diverse stakeholders in the design and testing process – undertake thorough user research and public engagement, ensuring that you include the views of those likely to be most affected by the project
    <ul>
      <li>this might include running co-design workshops or focus groups</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>complete an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA) – this can help to ensure that the project and its outcomes are fair and do not disadvantage protected groups</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>use feedback mechanisms, such as surveys and advisory boards, to enable stakeholders to continuously shape project outcomes – this can help to reduce any negative impacts across the project life cycle</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>make sure you have meaningful human control at the right stages – having human oversight of AI systems can help to maintain accountability and correct any erroneous or potentially harmful impacts</p>
  </li>
  <li>continuously evaluate and improve the project to ensure it’s meeting user needs and its intended use, by asking:
    <ul>
      <li>at the beginning of the project, are we doing the right thing?</li>
      <li>during the project, have we designed it well and how can we improve?</li>
      <li>after the project, is it still doing the thing we designed it for, and if it’s no longer serving a purpose, is there a process or decommissioning the system with minimal impact on end users?</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="safety-section">Safety</h2>

<p>In the context of data and data-driven technologies, safety refers to themes such as accuracy, security, reliability and robustness. It also covers topics such as the safety of researchers and research participants, and safe personal data collection and management.</p>

<p>In the context of AI, safety means ensuring that a system performs as intended across its life cycle, even in unexpected circumstances. This is particularly important in high-risk areas such as healthcare, policing and justice.</p>

<p>The scale and criticality of government services means they have the potential to cause widespread harm if they’re not designed with safety in mind.</p>

<p>If data-driven systems are not built safely, they can:</p>

<ul>
  <li>perform poorly and produce incorrect results</li>
  <li>cause harm to individuals and society</li>
  <li>reduce trust in public services and organisations</li>
</ul>

<p>Important concepts for data and AI safety are:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>accuracy – making sure that data is accurate and high quality, and that AI systems perform accurately</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>security – protecting data and AI systems against unauthorised access, tampering and leakage</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>reliability – ensuring that data pipelines and AI systems consistently deliver acceptable and expected results in all expected scenarios across the duration of use and deployment</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>robustness – designing data infrastructure and AI systems to withstand unexpected inputs, adversarial attacks and failures across the duration of its deployment</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>protection from harm – data use and AI systems must not cause harm to individuals, society or the planet</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>controllability – maintaining human oversight over data and AI systems, including the ability to intervene and align outcomes with societal values</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Find out more about AI safety principles in the Alan Turing Institute’s <a rel="external" href="https://aiethics.turing.ac.uk/modules/safety/">guidance on AI Safety in Practice</a> and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/understanding-artificial-intelligence-ethics-and-safety">Understanding artificial intelligence ethics and safety</a>.</p>

<h3 id="what-safety-means-in-practice">What safety means in practice</h3>

<p>Safety considerations can emerge across a project life cycle – from initial research and data collection, to the downstream impacts of a system.</p>

<p>In the context of data collection, sharing and use, safety means:</p>

<ul>
  <li>ensuring data is only used for lawful purposes</li>
  <li>handling data in a way that protects individuals’ privacy and minimises harm</li>
  <li>ensuring data is of high quality</li>
  <li>using secure systems for storing and processing data</li>
  <li>applying appropriate anonymisation techniques</li>
</ul>

<p>In the context of data-driven tools and AI systems, safety means:</p>

<ul>
  <li>designing data-driven systems that work as expected and do not cause harm</li>
  <li>testing systems to make sure they perform accurately and reliably under unexpected conditions</li>
  <li>keeping systems secure and protecting them from misuse</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="start-with-safe-research">Start with safe research</h4>

<p>Research is vital to design a project responsibly and robustly, and make sure that systems and products meet user needs. Research can help you understand fairness issues and build trust.</p>

<p>Research and data collection are often essential for improving government services and shaping new projects. But both quantitative and qualitative research can carry risks for participants.</p>

<p>You must consider the safety of both researchers and participants before starting a project. You should have safeguards in place and maintain them for as long as needed.</p>

<p>Qualitative research can carry risks if not planned carefully. This type of research involves collecting non-numerical data, such as:</p>

<ul>
  <li>interviews </li>
  <li>focus groups</li>
  <li>direct observations</li>
</ul>

<p>The safety of research participants in qualitative research is critical. Participants may be at risk of harm or distress, especially if the research involves sensitive topics. There may also be risks to their physical safety – for example, if taking part causes tension within their community or social group.</p>

<h4 id="reduce-risks-for-participants">Reduce risks for participants</h4>

<p>You must take steps to protect research participants. This applies to your team and to any third-party researchers you work with. </p>

<p>You should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>make sure that participants understand the research and any risks involved </li>
  <li>only include participants who give clear, informed consent without pressure or coercion </li>
  <li>allow participants to withdraw at any time (with exceptions for situations like medical research where participant information is anonymised and aggregated and cannot be removed from the research data set)</li>
  <li>anonymise all data used in reports or analysis </li>
</ul>

<p>Anonymising qualitative data can be difficult. Even if names, places or dates are removed, the detail in participants’ stories may still make them identifiable. You should take extra steps to protect their identity. The Service Manual has guidance on <a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy">managing user research data and participant privacy</a>.</p>

<h3 id="reduce-risks-for-researchers">Reduce risks for researchers</h3>

<p>Some research projects involve sensitive topics, such as child protection or adult safeguarding. These can be distressing for both researchers and participants. To reduce risk, you should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>highlight any sensitive topics in workshop or interview plans</li>
  <li>set up a ‘safety check-in’ protocol to support staff after sessions, particularly for one-to-one or lone working</li>
  <li>use existing ethical guidelines and processes, such as the Service Manual’s guidance on <a href="https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/researching-emotionally-sensitive-subjects">researching emotionally sensitive subjects</a>
</li>
</ul>

<p>In rare cases, researchers may be targeted by participants or others. If this happens, or if the risk is known in advance, put safeguards in place to protect staff.</p>

<p>The Government Analysis Function provides <a rel="external" href="https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/">a list of resources</a> related to conducting research and analysis in government.</p>

<h4 id="safe-data-collection-and-management">Safe data collection and management</h4>

<p>There are several safety risks related to the collection and management of data, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>poor data quality – including incomplete data, duplicated data, and insufficient or poor-quality metadata</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>data leakage – the unauthorised exposure of personal or sensitive information</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>data drift – the changes in the statistical properties of real-world data distributions over time, which can affect the performance of machine learning models trained on historical data</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>data poisoning – a malicious act where a hacker compromises data sources during collection and pre-processing by introducing corrupted data</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Data security principles and processes are required the moment you begin collecting data. Limiting the amount and sensitivity of data that you collect reduces the potential for harm if data is exposed. Principles like data minimisation, as covered in the <a href="#privacy-section">Privacy</a> section, are relevant to safety and security.</p>

<p>Loss or theft of personal data can have wide-reaching legal and financial consequences. It can also cause significant psychological harm to people affected. Working directly or indirectly with data in the public sector comes with a duty to protect the personal data you hold about individuals. Refer to the government’s <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services">personal data security principles</a> when processing and sharing personal data.</p>

<p>If you’re working with any third-party suppliers to store, collect or process data, make sure they’re vetted and that they comply with the security requirements of your project. There’s guidance on security measures for AI systems in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government">AI Playbook for the UK Government.</a> </p>

<h4 id="ensure-data-is-fit-for-purpose">Ensure data is fit for purpose</h4>

<p>All civil servants have a responsibility to ensure that the data they manage and use is of high quality and fit for purpose. Data quality should be checked and validated across the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework/the-government-data-quality-framework#The-Data-Lifecycle">data life cycle</a>. This includes ensuring data is fit for purpose before, during and after data analysis or model development and deployment.</p>

<p>Refer to the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework">Government Data Quality Framework</a> for guidance on understanding, documenting and improving data quality, and for information about real public sector case studies. The framework sets out the main dimensions of data quality, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>completeness</li>
  <li>uniqueness</li>
  <li>consistency</li>
  <li>timeliness</li>
  <li>validity</li>
  <li>accuracy</li>
</ul>

<p>Maintaining data quality is a continuous process. You should maintain clear documentation of any known limitations, biases and quality concerns. If using data for analysis and model development, you should conduct ongoing validation of outputs, especially where models are reused or retrained.</p>

<p>Tools such as data sheets or data set cards can be helpful in documenting information about data quality. The <a href="#transparency-section">Transparency</a> section has more information on this.</p>

<h4 id="data-and-model-poisoning">Data and model poisoning</h4>

<p>Data poisoning, otherwise known as AI or model poisoning, is a type of cyberattack that involves hackers modifying or introducing new data points into a training data set.</p>

<p>Data poisoning attacks can be direct or indirect. Direct attacks involve deliberately manipulating a machine learning model to behave in a particular way. Indirect attacks aim to degrade the performance of models more generally. This could include inserting irrelevant or incorrect data into a training set, reducing model accuracy.</p>

<p>It can be difficult to determine if and how data poisoning has taken place, particularly when using an AI model from a third-party source. For example, poisoned models may function as expected until triggered by a specific prompt or scenario.</p>

<p>Data poisoning can occur in different ways across the data and AI life cycle, such as:</p>

<ul>
  <li>collecting and using data from uncontrollable or unreliable sources, like social media or Internet of Things (IoT) devices</li>
  <li>weak access controls </li>
  <li>malicious actors modifying training data labels to reflect wrong information</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="a-data-poisoning-example">A data poisoning example</h4>

<p>A company builds a voice assistant that helps users control smart devices. To improve the system, the company invites users to help by transcribing voice recordings.</p>

<p>A competitor finds out about this and deliberately mislabels thousands of recordings. For example, they label recordings of users saying “turn the lights off” as “turn the lights on”.</p>

<p>Over time, the system learns the wrong behaviour. After an update, the AI assistant starts turning lights on when users ask for them to be turned off, and vice versa. This leads to a poor user experience and damages the company’s reputation.</p>

<h4 id="the-impact-of-data-poisoning">The impact of data poisoning</h4>

<p>The impacts of an AI model trained or fine-tuned with poisoned data are wide-ranging, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>security threats to the organisation deploying the model</li>
  <li>biased or harmful outputs being sent to users </li>
  <li>poor system performance and accuracy, such as misclassification</li>
</ul>

<p>Reducing the risk of data poisoning should include technical safeguards and clear policies for data management.</p>

<p>Example steps include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>using encryption and strict access controls to prevent unauthorised access to systems and data sets
    <ul>
      <li>the Information Commissioner’s Office has <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/security/encryption/">guidance on encryption</a>
</li>
      <li>industry-standard encryption methods and protocols, such as advanced encryption standards (AES 256) and Transport Layer Security/Secure Socket Layer (TLS/SSL), also apply to AI systems, data sets and models</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>conducting supply chain checks, as poisoned models often originate from pre-trained models that have been fine-tuned using poisoned or compromised data sources</li>
  <li>implementing strong validation techniques to check data set quality and accuracy – methods such as anomaly detection can help to detect abnormal outliers and extreme data points</li>
  <li>monitoring and auditing systems for signs of unusual behaviour, such as sudden drops in system performance</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="building-safe-ai-systems">Building safe AI systems</h3>

<p>AI systems can behave in unexpected ways, especially if they’re designed poorly or deployed without adequate testing. Many AI systems work in complex and unpredictable environments. This makes it harder to build systems that are safe and reliable.</p>

<p>Elements to consider in the context of AI safety include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>safety of data – ensuring that data used for AI model training and AI system operation is accurate, high quality and legally compliant
    <ul>
      <li>this should include testing data for anomalies, identifying and addressing harmful biases, and documenting information about data sets</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>safety of the AI model – ensuring that the model is technically robust and reliable, and performs accurately even in unexpected conditions
    <ul>
      <li>consider testing and measuring model performance on validation data sets against metrics such as accuracy and precision, and fairness metrics</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>safety of the AI system – ensuring that the AI system functions safely and as intended within its wider context, including with users and other systems
    <ul>
      <li>continually monitor for unusual behaviour post-deployment, including any potentially harmful outputs</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>You should prioritise the technical objectives of accuracy, reliability, security and robustness from the outset. Building an AI system that meets these objectives requires testing, validation and re-assessment throughout its entire life cycle. It also requires maintaining human oversight and control.</p>

<p>You should run rigorous testing to identify potential failure modes for AI systems. This may include using semi-automated techniques, such as using adversarial models to develop prompts, or red teaming exercises, to record how models behave under unexpected scenarios.</p>

<p>If it’s not possible to make the system sufficiently safe for the intended use, even with available mitigations, because of the potential risks or failure modes, you should not use the system to address the problem.</p>

<p>If using off-the-shelf generative AI tools, you will likely need to put additional guardrails in place, such as pre- and post-prompt filters. While no generative AI system can be guaranteed to be entirely safe, these measures, combined with ongoing testing and monitoring, can help reduce risks to an acceptable level.</p>

<p>Consider adopting the following practices to make AI systems safer and more secure:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>be transparent – you should document information about models, data sets and system prompts, and make sure operators understand how the system works in different situations</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>design for resilience – use backup components for critical functions so that the system can continue operating safely even if one element fails</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>apply least privilege principles – distribute responsibility and prevent any single person from having too much control or access</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>build in risk controls – build in ways for the system to slow down or stop if it starts to behave in unexpected or unusual ways</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>establish multiple system defences – apply multiple safety measures rather than relying on just one, including a human-in-the-loop to review outputs</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>continually evaluate security factors – you should continually reassess factors that might impact security, including training data sets, model complexity and supply chains</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Find out more about AI safety and security in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-cyber-security-code-of-practice/code-of-practice-for-the-cyber-security-of-ai">Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI</a> and the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) <a rel="external" href="https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/guidelines-secure-ai-system-development">guidelines for secure AI system development</a>.</p>

<p>There’s also guidance in the:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/introduction-to-ai-assurance/introduction-to-ai-assurance">Introduction to AI Assurance</a> which explores AI assurance techniques</li>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/responsible-ai-toolkit#:~:text=This%20toolkit%20of%20guidance%20aims,over%20time%20with%20new%20resources.">Responsible AI Toolkit</a> which lists various resources that support the safe and responsible development and deployment of AI systems</li>
  <li>
<a rel="external" href="https://testing-ai-standards.github.io/cross-gov-ai-testing-framework/">AI Testing and Assurance Framework for Public Sector</a> which sets out a practical approach for testing, evaluation and assurance of AI systems</li>
  <li>
<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html">AI Playbook for the UK Government</a> for information about the security and safety of AI systems</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="recommended-actions-6">Recommended actions</h3>

<p>Your team should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>make sure researchers and research participants are physically and emotionally safe – consider how a research topic could cause distress or discomfort, and reduce these risks by providing clear information, gaining informed consent, and allowing participants to withdraw at any time</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>comply with security requirements and standards – new services, including AI systems, must comply with the government’s <a rel="external" href="https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/">Secure by Design principles</a> which help ensure that systems are secure throughout their life cycle</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>apply data minimisation to limit the potential harms of a data breach – this means processing only the minimum amount of personal data necessary to achieve your purpose</p>
  </li>
  <li>keep all data secure throughout the project, referring to the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services">personal data security principles</a>
</li>
  <li>check for issues that could affect data quality, accuracy or reliability, such as data drift or model poisoning, by referring to the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework">Government Data Quality Framework</a>
</li>
  <li>
    <p>ensure human oversight and have strategies to intervene where necessary, especially in high-risk use cases of AI, so that humans can validate decisions and outputs</p>
  </li>
  <li>run rigorous testing to identify potential failure modes for AI systems 
    <ul>
      <li>this may include using semi-automated techniques, such as using adversarial models to develop prompts, or red teaming exercises</li>
      <li>if it’s not possible to make the system sufficiently safe for the intended use, you should not use it to address the problem</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>use available resources, including the <a rel="external" href="https://learn.civilservice.gov.uk/courses/f7Sf3JPkTQiwYgr2qatDEw">courses on risks and ethics on Civil Service Learning</a> and the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html">AI Playbook</a>
</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="further-resources">Further resources</h2>

<p>There’s a range of <a href="https://www.gov.uk/data-ethics-guidance">data ethics guidance, standards and frameworks</a> developed by and for government and public sector bodies. These resources support the responsible use and development of data and data-driven technologies, including AI.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/responsible-ai-toolkit">Responsible AI Toolkit</a> also lists guidance related to deploying AI systems.</p>

<p>The UK Statistics Authority provides <a rel="external" href="https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/what-we-do/data-ethics/centre-for-applied-data-ethics/guidance-and-support/ethics-guidance-documents/">guidance related to applied data ethics</a> in research and statistics.</p>

<p>Here are some other public sector resources.</p>

<h4 id="ai-knowledge-hub">AI Knowledge Hub</h4>
<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://ai.gov.uk/knowledge-hub/">AI Knowledge Hub</a> brings together guidance and case studies for teams adopting AI technologies in the public sector.</p>

<h4 id="ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government">AI Playbook for the UK Government</h4>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government">AI Playbook</a> offers guidance on using AI safely, effectively and securely for civil servants and people working in government organisations.</p>

<h4 id="algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-atrs">Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (<abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr>)</h4>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub"><abbr title="Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard">ATRS</abbr></a> provides a standardised way for public bodies to document information about algorithmic tools used in decision-making processes which impact the public.</p>

<h4 id="analytical-quality-assurance-book-aqua">Analytical Quality Assurance Book (<abbr title="Analytical Quality Assurance Book">AQuA</abbr>)</h4>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-aqua-book"><abbr title="Analytical Quality Assurance Book">AQuA</abbr> Book</a> is a best practice guide for civil servants working with analysis and analytical models.</p>

<h4 id="data-sharing-governance-framework">Data Sharing Governance Framework</h4>
<p>This <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-sharing-governance-framework/data-sharing-governance-framework">framework</a> is one of a growing suite of tools which enable better use, reuse and sharing of data across government.</p>

<h4 id="government-data-quality-framework">Government Data Quality Framework</h4>
<p>This <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-data-quality-framework">guidance</a> sets out principles and practices to assess, communicate and improve the quality of data in government. Linked with this, there’s guidance on <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/implementing-a-data-quality-action-plan">implementing a data quality action plan</a>.</p>

<h4 id="dstl-biscuit-book--assurance-of-ai-and-autonomous-systems">
<abbr title="Defence Science and Technology Laboratory">Dstl</abbr> biscuit book – Assurance of AI and Autonomous Systems</h4>
<p>This is a <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/assurance-of-ai-and-autonomous-systems-a-dstl-biscuit-book">guide</a> to understanding and describing the trustworthiness of autonomous systems and associated AI algorithms. It was written by the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (<abbr title="Defence Science and Technology Laboratory">Dstl</abbr>).</p>

<h4 id="explaining-decisions-made-with-ai">Explaining decisions made with AI</h4>
<p>This <a rel="external" href="https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/explaining-decisions-made-with-artificial-intelligence/">guidance</a> is from the Information Commissioner’s Office and the Alan Turing Institute. It gives organisations practical advice to help explain the processes, services and decisions delivered or assisted by AI, to the individuals affected by them.</p>

<h4 id="five-safes-framework">Five Safes framework</h4>
<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/secure-lab/what-is-the-five-safes-framework/">Five Safes framework</a> is a set of principles which enable data services to provide safe research access to data.</p>

<h4 id="guidelines-for-ai-procurement">Guidelines for AI Procurement</h4>
<p>Use these <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidelines-for-ai-procurement/guidelines-for-ai-procurement">guidelines</a> when procuring AI-powered solutions.</p>

<h4 id="model-for-responsible-innovation">Model for Responsible Innovation </h4>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-model-for-responsible-innovation/the-model-for-responsible-innovation">Model for Responsible Innovation</a> is a practical tool created by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). It helps teams across the public sector and beyond to innovate responsibly with data and AI. You can use the model to run red teaming workshops with teams developing data-driven technology.</p>

<h4 id="pets-adoption-guide">PETs Adoption Guide</h4>
<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://cdeiuk.github.io/pets-adoption-guide/adoption-guide/">PETs Adoption Guide</a> provides an interactive flowchart to help decision makers determine which privacy enhancing technologies (PETs) might be useful for their project. The guide is primarily aimed at technical architects and product owners working on projects that involve the sharing or processing of sensitive information.</p>

<h4 id="portfolio-of-ai-assurance-techniques">Portfolio of AI assurance techniques</h4>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/ai-assurance-techniques">portfolio of AI assurance techniques</a> provides a searchable repository of cross-industry AI assurance techniques.</p>

<h4 id="technology-code-of-practice">Technology Code of Practice</h4>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-technology-code-of-practice">Technology Code of Practice</a> is a set of criteria to help the government design, build and buy technology.</p>

<h4 id="uksa-ethics-self-assessment-tool">UKSA Ethics Self-Assessment Tool</h4>
<p>The <a rel="external" href="https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/the-authority-board/committees/national-statisticians-advisory-committees-and-panels/national-statisticians-data-ethics-advisory-committee/ethics-self-assessment-tool/#pid-archived-guidance">Ethics Self-Assessment Tool</a> developed by the UK Statistics Authority gives researchers an easy-to-use framework to review the ethics of their projects throughout the research cycle.</p>
